title: ‘Dune: Part Three’ Smashes BFI Imax Record With 33,000 Admissions Sold In First 24 Hours
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Armie Hammer Wraps Under-The-Radar Action Thriller ‘Tokyo Blitz’; Film Heads To AFM For Sales Sony Wins Rights In Host Of International Territories To A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Primetime’ Patrick Schwarzenegger To Lead AGC Crime Thriller ‘The Journeyman’; Leslie Grace Also Set View All October 21, 2026 7:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani in 'Dune: Part Three' Warner Bros. BFI IMAX , the UK’s largest screen, has sold 33,000 advance tickets for Dune: Part Three i n 24 hours, breaking first day presale records for the venue with a total gross of more than £880,000 ($988,000). This follows three opening weekend screenings that had previously sold out in under an hour last April, and two previews that also sold out earlier this month. The BFI, which will show the film in IMAX 70mm, saw unprecedented demand this summer for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , which was sold out for months at the screen. Dune , which releases in December, could be on course for similar success. DUNE: PART THREE (Denis Villeneuve, 2026) – £880,000 2. THE ODYSSEY (Christopher Nolan, 2026) – £750,000 3. DUNE: PART TWO (Denis Villeneuve, 2024) – £366,000 4. OPPENHEIMER (Christopher Nolan, 2023) – £254,000 5. AVATAR: FIRE AND ASH (James Cameron, 2025) – £116,000 The BFI screen will show Dune (2021) and Dune: Part Two (2024), the latter projected from an IMAX 70mm print, when both return to the UK’s largest screen from Friday 11 December. Preview screenings of Dune: Part Three begin at BFI IMAX in IMAX 70mm from Tuesday 15 December. Set nearly two decades after the previous instalment, Denis Villeneuve’s latest chapter in the space saga starring Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya sees “Paul Atreides face the consequences of his reign as old allies return, terrifying new threats emerge, and betrayal lurks in every shadow. Haunted by visions of Imperial collapse and the reappearance of Chani, Paul is drawn into a sweeping conspiracy, with his long-lost love at the heart of its unfolding mystery. When enemies close in, Paul must confront the true cost of power and the fate of those he loves the most.” Dune Part: Two (2024) grossed $714M across its run. The Odyssey this year took a whopping $1.8BN with a large chunk coming from PLF screens. By mid August alone, the BFI IMAX had sold more than 100,000 admissions for the movie, generating £2,683,987 gross in ticket sales from a single screen and achieving a 95% occupancy rate across all showtimes at the time – making it the cinema’s highest grossing film ever. title: The Emancipation of Charli D’Amelio: How the TikTok Queen Took Back Her Life
full_text: Skip to main content By Nancy Jo Sales Plus Icon Nancy Jo Sales View All October 21, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Charli D’Amelio was photographed Oct. 5 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Artisitic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Prada dress, top, jewelry. Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ruffly black gown. “So pretty, stunning,” says Emman Montalvan, the photographer snapping her. “Gorg!” With her glossy black hair and sparkly smile, Charli is gorg. She’s the girl next door drawn by Disney; she’s the bright and shiny face of social media , making it all seem benign. “This is her before she becomes jaded,” Montalvan observes. “Nothing calculated. Natural. She reminds me of when Britney Spears was young.” Related Stories THR Cover Story Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G Business Instagram Lines Up Donatella Versace, A$AP Rocky, Finneas, Chloé Zhao as This Year's Creator Awards Judges (Exclusive) Rihanna’s “Breakin’ Dishes” begins to play. Charli mouths the words: “I don’t know who you think I am —” “Are you having fun?” I ask, finding myself smiling. Because when Charli is happy, you feel happy — which is no doubt part of her appeal. You want to believe that a life spent dancing around in fabulous clothes and opening yourself up to a dizzying 160 million-plus followers (the second most on TikTok) really is as wonderful as it looks. But a flicker of annoyance crosses Charli’s brow, as if the question touches a nerve. Maybe that’s because of how the algorithms are always demanding she offer up the semblance of a perfect life, the performance of joy, no matter the reality. “Are you having fun?” she asks, flashing her diamond bracelet smile. Then she’s running gleefully down the hallway of the studio, followed by her social media manager, Alexa Davis, who films her nearly constantly with a DJI Osmo Pocket. When Charli’s having fun, there’s someone there to capture it. *** Coming off a 10-month run in Broadway’s & Juliet — in which she sang and danced in the ensemble cast, earning some good reviews — Charli moved into a house in Valley Village, California, all by herself, earlier this year. The place represents something more than just a first home: At 22, Charli has separated herself professionally and financially from the family with whom she built her extraordinary career. “I’m figuring out who I want to be,” she tells me, “and that’s what I’m really excited for.” Photographed by Emman Montalvan For years, Charli and her parents, Marc and Heidi D’Amelio, and her older sister, Dixie, seemed inseparable. They moved to L.A. together, signed with the same talent agency, started businesses, starred in a Hulu reality show. Charli was always the main attraction, the engine of an empire — consisting of brand partnerships, media ventures, a clothing line and more — all built on the image of a close-knit family. Now, amid public speculation that her parents mismanaged her money — which her father has denied — she’s trying to find out who she is apart from them. (None of the D’Amelios responded to requests for comment.) The new place is her first house of her own. It doesn’t quite look like what you’d expect of a young woman who earns an estimated $18 million a year annually, according to Forbes . It’s a modest, almost nondescript two-story house on a tree-lined street, with a gate and security door, but nothing that screams “TikTok star.” But then you get to the secluded backyard with its shimmering pool, immaculate lawn and big stone grill, and you see the dance studio with the neon sign: RED BULL DANCE YOUR STYLE. Red Bull, one of Charli’s sponsors, built it for her. She grew up promoting brands; now even her backyard comes with one. “This is a very much a home,” Charli says, her voice soft and gentle as ASMR. She’s sitting cross-legged on the oversized wraparound couch in her big, open living room — her “safe space,” she tells me. She’s wearing Levi’s and a long-sleeved black Prada top (she’s an official friend of the house, so there’s Prada, Prada everywhere around her). Seventeen silver studs and hoops glint at her ears. “Sometimes I just fall asleep here,” she says sleepily. “It’s so comfy, it’s a slippery slope.” She spends a lot of time alone, just being on her phone or watching her giant, wall-mounted TV. On the couch, there’s a pillow that says: JUST A GIRL WHO LOVES ORCAS. Charli says she likes the way they always win in a fight with sharks. “Lame of a life as it may be sometimes, I love just to be at home and do nothing,” she says. “I’m surrounded by a lot of peace, which is something it took me a long time to realize I need to be comfortable.” She’s been a bit of a “hermit” over the past year, she says, retreating from a life in which almost everything she did was potentially something to be shared. “I took my first break off of social media” between October and February, “which was a really tough decision — I was always told, ‘If you take a break, you can never come back’ — but I think mentally I was just in a place where I needed to stop working and figure out who I was. Photographed by Emman Montalvan “I started working full-time when I was 15,” she continues, “and once I started, it was, ‘OK, this is my life now.’ But the other side of it was, ‘This is all I’ve ever known.’ And I think it took me, really for the first time, taking a step back and being like, ‘Who am I? What am I? Do I have a favorite color? Do I have a favorite anything?’ I realized I didn’t really know anything about myself, and so I had to sit with the hard truth of like, ‘Who am I at night when everyone leaves and no one cares that I’m Charli D’Amelio,’ you know?” Her dog, Rebel, a 12-year-old chocolate lab, stares up at her worshipfully. The bloodshot eyes of the internet noticed, of course, when Charli took a break — not just from social media but seemingly from the family that had been so central to her identity. She hasn’t appeared publicly with her parents or her sister for about a year, adding to speculation of a rift. In May, the gossip website Deuxmoi published allegations that Marc and Heidi had mismanaged Charli’s money. In June, Marc took to TikTok to deny these claims. “So a website said … we took money and put it offshore,” said Marc, sounding frustrated. “I wouldn’t even know how to do that. Come on, dude. This was never about money, it was about having this crazy, awesome experience with my family.” And then in September, appearing on creator Quenlin Blackwell’s YouTube cooking show, Feeding Starving Celebrities, Charli was asked how much money she had made from a certain item of merch. “Mmm, ain’t that the question,” she responded, deadpan. “Wouldn’t I like to know.” The moment went viral, becoming a GIF. “Charli D’Amelio family drama” trended on TikTok. *** Photographed by Emman Montalvan Charli was just your average upper-middle-class girl, growing up in Norwalk, Connecticut, when TikTok made her famous overnight. She’d been dancing competitively for nearly a decade when, in May 2019, at age 15, she began posting videos of herself doing popular routines, “just like everybody else was doing.” “My dream in life was to be a backup dancer,” she says. “I was like, ‘I want to go to the University of Nevada at Las Vegas and join their dance team,’ because they’d won nationals. I’m a very type A person. I had a vision board — I had a whole plan. But then the plan went sideways.” Five months after she started posting on TikTok, she had a million followers. By November 2020, she’d become the first TikTok creator to reach 100 million. Why her? Even Charli can’t explain it. “I think it was a mix of things,” she says. “Happy accident.” People watched her videos repeatedly to learn the choreography. “Also, when I started, I got just as much hate as I got love, so people were talking, arguing with each other.” Enragement, as they say, drove engagement. People argued about Charli’s looks, her dancing, whether she deserved her fame. In 2019, she drew criticism for performing the viral “Renegade” dance to K Camp’s song “Lottery” without crediting its 14-year-old Black creator, Jalaiah Harmon. (Charli and pop star Addison Rae later performed the original choreography with Harmon, giving her proper credit.) Then COVID-19 drove young people inside, where they were more often on their phones, and what better way to distract oneself from a pandemic than watching pretty Charli D’Amelio dance? For a generation of girls, Charli represented the ultimate social media success story. You didn’t need a Hollywood agent — you could become famous in your bedroom, just by being yourself. The catch: Once being yourself became your job, you might never get to stop working. Charli was about to become one of the most famous teenagers in the world while remaining remarkably powerless over her own life, she says: “I was a child, which I didn’t really get the significance of at the time, but I can see it very clearly now.” In summer 2020, Charli moved with her family into a rented mansion in the Hollywood Hills. The relocation was her idea; she felt “there was a lot more I could be doing,” though she’d already appeared in a Super Bowl commercial and an ABC special. She and her family signed with UTA as a package. Marc came from the apparel industry and had an unsuccessful run as a Republican candidate for the Connecticut State Senate in 2018; Heidi was a former model and personal trainer; and Dixie, three years older than Charli, was an aspiring singer. The family seemed to envision a Kardashian-esque enterprise, with Charli as its teenage Kim. Marc and Dixie launched their own TikTok accounts after Charli went viral. Everyone had a part to play in Charli’s newfound fame. Photographed by Emman Montalvan There’s a family story here that predates TikTok: A gifted child gets flooded with opportunities, and the adults around her see ways to capitalize on her appeal. Their involvement in her career, no matter how well-meaning, also gives them a say in her image and her decisions. In the pilot episode of The D’Amelio Show (2021-2023), the family sits down to hear the business plan for the upcoming year. Greg Goodfried, a former UTA agent who became their manager, holds forth enthusiastically. On the floor are 23 binders — 23! — containing proposals for a slew of new business ventures. Charli looks scared. “Where is the binder where she gets to be a kid?” Heidi asks. “I still have those binders,” Charli tells me wryly. “Twenty-three major projects in a year were agreed to. I had just turned 16.” (Goodfried did not respond to requests for comment.) Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** “I’m always grateful. I know I’m very lucky,” Charli says. “I don’t know what doing this without them would have looked like; I don’t know if I would have had this life.” It’s a refrain she returns to, almost as if she fears that questioning what happened will be mistaken for ingratitude. One of the peculiar cruelties of fame for young women is that they must be grateful for it, no matter how much it hurts. But lately she’s been reassessing what it meant to be a working child in the entertainment industry. “I was the youngest in every room I was in,” she says. “I was surrounded by people who were the best in the business, so you trust because that’s all you have — these people who are supposed to be guiding and helping you. But people are selfish, and that’s the sad reality. “And people have bad intentions, too,” she adds. “You can’t be a trusting person. I’ve learned that the hard way.” Rebel presses her nose against Charli’s knee. Charli pats it. “There are not a lot of rules and regulations when it comes to people who do what I do,” says Charli. “I didn’t start learning about and getting involved in my financials until I was about 21. I’m very fortunate to be able to be living the life that I am, but I’ve also been working nonstop since I was 15, so I should have stuff to show for it.” The laws protecting children in film and television evolved over decades in response to cases of exploitation. But the business of children making money on social media has grown faster than the rules protecting them. When parents are also business partners, who is looking out for the child? Are the rumors true, I ask, about her parents mishandling her money? “No, they’re not true,” Charli says. “I wouldn’t say that they stole my money.” There’s a long pause. “I think we did a lot of things as a family,” she says carefully. Photographed by Emman Montalvan *** Recently, Charli has been watching The D’Amelio Show for the first time. “It’s kind of like watching something I never lived,” she says. “It’s almost as if I’m figuring out what has happened in my life over these last few years. I was so disconnected in so many ways.” I mention how flat and monotone she seems onscreen, nothing like the person talking to me now. “I was like that. For years,” she says. “I kind of stopped talking. I stopped having a personality. I stopped doing much of anything because I had so much scrutiny from the outside world. It’s taken me to now to realize maybe I was dissociating through a lot of it.” All 28 episodes of The D’Amelio Show come with mental health trigger warnings. Charli and Dixie are seen struggling with the unceasing abuse that comes with online fame. At one point, a viral post predicts Charli’s death. Grown men make vulgar, sexualized videos about her when she’s still a teenager. “It’s a scary world, and it was hard on me,” she says. Her experience wasn’t so different from that of millions of girls negotiating a world of constant comparison and judgment — it was just on a much larger scale. Charli was the smiling face of a platform that amplified those pressures, twerking and twirling like the girl in The Red Shoes who couldn’t stop dancing. To many of her fans, she represented the fantasy: beauty, popularity, incredible clothes, a seemingly perfect family, wealth that came from doing what she loved. Behind it was a girl overwhelmed by scrutiny. Adolescent girls had always been judged on their looks and popularity; what was new was the technology that could make the judgment relentless, public and profitable. Charli was both a victim of social media culture and one of its most effective advertisements. “Have you ever seen The Matrix ?” I ask. “Is that the one where Keanu Reeves goes like this?” she says, doing the move where he dodges bullets in slow motion. I tell her about the main character, Neo, who discovers his world is a simulation controlled by machines. “And then when he wakes up, he starts fighting back. You should watch it.” “I love that, you’re giving me homework,” she says with a little laugh. Charli had suffered from anxiety even before TikTok. “I was a kid when I started having severe anxiety,” she says. In third grade, bullies pulled her hair and shoved her into a bathroom stall, breaking two of her fingers. “That was the same age I started having anxiety, so maybe they are connected,” she says. “I never really thought about that before.” On her reality show, her anxiety becomes a storyline. She describes having up to 15 panic attacks a day; viewers see her sob and break down in response to online hate. “But then I would get hate for showing my feelings,” she says. “You’re not allowed to be upset, you’re not allowed to cry, you’re not allowed to have any emotion, you can’t be angry.” Part of the concept of the show was to expose the dark side of influencer fame — even as it made its underage star more famous. But while the show urged viewers who were struggling to seek treatment for their mental health, Charli feels she didn’t always get the help she needed. “I went untreated for most of my life,” she says. “I had a life coach” from ages 16 to 19, “but I didn’t have a therapist. I probably should have had a therapist. I wasn’t medicated at all, even though I had ADHD, which I didn’t get diagnosed with until I was 18.” She was later also diagnosed with OCD and trichotillomania, a hair-pulling disorder associated with OCD and anxiety. Her life was work. Due to her professional commitments, she dropped out of high school at 16, though friends back home in Connecticut made sure she went to prom. Meanwhile, she was having experiences some kids dream of, such as winning season 31 of Dancing With the Stars (along with her dance partner Mark Ballas) in 2022, when she was 18. Her mother, Heidi, also competed that year. She came in eighth place. *** Matt Winkelmeyer/Kca2021/Getty Images for Nickelodeon/Tyler Golden/Hulu Charli has been seeing a therapist lately. “I told my therapist,” she says, “one thing I don’t want to be is another statistic. I don’t want to be another kid who got thrown into Hollywood and let that ruin their life.” The cautionary tales of child stardom, from Judy Garland to Britney Spears, have found a new breeding ground online. Charli’s generation doesn’t need studio executives to make them famous anymore, but the disappearance of the old gatekeepers hasn’t made children any less vulnerable to exploitation. I ask what finally made her reconsider how she wanted to move forward? “This is probably going to sound really crazy,” Charli says, “but I was doing Broadway” — & Juliet, a gig she’d chosen herself — “and it was the easiest thing I had ever done. And I did a good job. I showed up every day with a smile on my face, and I loved every second of it. And it reignited something in me, this love that I used to have” for dancing, performing. She had moved to New York — without her family — and was living in Columbus Circle to be near the theater. After years of being the star, it felt like a “relief” to be part of an ensemble of dancers, some of whom became friends. For the first time in her life, she was on her own, and it felt good. But then, when her run ended in September 2025, she says she became “the most depressed I’d ever been.” She rarely left her apartment and “didn’t see another human for a few months.” She went off social media and decided it was time to “take a look at myself.” Her team continued pitching projects that felt uncomfortably familiar. She started saying no. In December, she parted ways with Goodfried, her former manager. She doesn’t have a replacement manager yet, “but I’m OK with that,” she says. “I like it. I’m in charge. Now I say what I’m doing and not doing.” She sits up a little as she says this, her drowsy voice suddenly more alive. She also separated herself from the D’Amelio family business. Now, she oversees her own finances. For most 22-year-olds, independence means getting a job and supporting oneself; for Charli, it has meant taking command of an empire she helped build before she was old enough to vote. The internet took note again when she and her parents unfollowed one another on Instagram. Marc said on TikTok that he now communicates with Charli “through her lawyer.” As for Dixie, Charli says, “I mean, that’s my sister. I’m going to love her till the day I die. But there are times where you’re figuring stuff out.” Charli’s still making TikToks, still dancing around, smiling, in cool clothes; and she’s vlogging more on her YouTube channel, which has around 9 million followers. “Sometimes I want to record my entire day,” she says. “And sometimes I talk about whatever people are asking for. People like to feel included.” She’s still looking for ways to monetize her platform, still promoting Dunkin’, which has named two drinks after her: The Charli (2020) and The Charli Cold Foam (2021). Charli isn’t trying to bring down TikTok or renounce the fortune that brought her here. She isn’t trying to escape the machine. She just wants to be the one at the controls. “I’m taking the last few months of 2026 to work on getting to a place where I’m doing things I’m really proud of,” she says. She has a major project to announce in November, something that “I hold dear to my heart.” She continues: “Because of being told so often I didn’t deserve where I was, I felt that way for a really long time. But I’m at the point now where I can see that, like, I’ve lived a pretty amazing life, and I’m getting what I feel is like my second chance to do this the way that I want to do it. “I love what I do,” she says. “I love the person that I’m turning out to be.” Charli’s publicist, Nicole Perez-Krueger, comes in the room and says it’s time to stop. Charli’s dinner guests are arriving — her social media manager, Davis; her day-to-day manager, Alison Scoon; her stylist, Carlee Barrow; her agent, Ali Berman, and Berman’s 7-year-old daughter, June. They really are her friends, Charli says. They bring the sides. Charli’s going to grill them steak. “How do you do your TikToks and stuff?” June asks. “I just dance what I feel and say what I feel,” Charli says with a smile. Her social media manager is filming again. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Empire Founder Ghazi Launches Supply Chain, New Rights Management/ Distribution Company for Independent Music
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 7:00am PT Empire Founder Ghazi Launches Supply Chain, New Rights Management/ Distribution Company for Independent Music By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Music Industry Moves: Barbara Cane, BMI’s VP of Worldwide Creative, to Retire After Five Decades 16 hours ago Cleo Sol Announces First-Ever North American Arena Tour Dates 24 hours ago Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ghazi , founder of the indie label and distribution giant Empire , has announced the launch of his newest company, Supply Chain, an independent B2B cloud-based distribution company for the global music industry, which encapsulates technology, distribution, operations, and commercial connectivity. Alongside the launch, the company announced two senior leadership appointments, with Craig May joining as SVP of marketing and Kristy May as SVP of business affairs. Supply Chain’s international headquarters are based in Amsterdam, one of Europe’s most-connected music and technology hubs. According to the announcement, the company’s goal is a huge one: to build the infrastructure that independent music runs on. “Its mission is to deliver the technology, expertise and commercial access needed to operate, grow and compete globally, in service of a broader vision of a world where independent music has the power to shape its own future,” the announcement reads. “The platform gives independent music businesses neutral, enterprise-grade infrastructure without requiring them to give up control of their catalog, data, client relationships or commercial choices.” Supply Chain launched in beta in 2025 and is now operational globally. Supply Chain is working with a variety of clients across the industry ecosystem, including a launch partnership with Beatport-owned Ampsuite, to power infrastructure expansion. Popular on Variety “There needs to be a fully fleshed-out rights management system that is also culturally nuanced,” Ghazi tells Variety. “The needs of an independent label in Brazil are not the same as an artist in India, which are not the same as a private equity company that’s invested $500 million in catalogs. Supply Chain can manage contracts, master royalties, publishing royalties, merch royalties, split payments and more. “It’s been a labor of love for five years,” he continues. “I wanted to build something as scale-able and as future-proof as possible. It introduces a lot of operational efficiencies and reduces tech friction, and when you do all that, you’re allowing creativity to flourish. Our software is built for independents and it’s designed to connect and serve the independent community.” Beatport CEO Matt Gralen says, “Ampsuite offers the most complete set of tools for the labels that power Beatport, but we are always looking to provide more and respond to evolution in the industry. title: Roku Streamer Howdy Buys ‘The Walsh Sisters’
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Roku Streamer Howdy Buys ‘The Walsh Sisters’ Russell Brand Told Fan To “Clean Up Mess” After Alleged Rape As Accuser Tells Court She “Carried Feeling Of Guilt & Shame” For Years Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Manager Spearheading Entertainment & New Media Biz At Three Six Zero View All October 21, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Walsh Sisters Leanne Sullivan EXCLUSIVE: Roku ‘s new streamer Howdy has boosted its offering with the acquisition of exclusive rights to hit BBC -RTÉ adaptation The Walsh Sisters . Starring Derry Girls actor Louisa Harland, the Marian Keyes adaptation follows five Irish sisters through secrets, family feuds and moments of grace. Howdy has landed Season 1 rights from November 5 exclusively in the U.S., with episodes dropping weekly, and will take Season 2 next year around the time The Walsh Sisters launches in the UK and Ireland. The Walsh Sisters , which is based on a hugely popular set of novels, has been a hit for the BBC and RTÉ. Caroline Menton ( Oddity ), Danielle Galligan ( House of Guinness ), Máiréad Tyers ( Extraordinary ), Stefanie Preissner (who also adapted the series), Aidan Quinn and Carrie Crowley also star. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News BBC Scraps TikTok Generation TV News Bulletin 'The Catch Up' Acquisitions The BBC & MHz Choice Board Sweden's Latest 'Wallander' Series The Walsh Sisters joins the likes of Weapons , Django Unchained and The Wicker Man on Howdy. Following its acquisition by Fox, Roku unveiled Howdy last year as a cheaper ad-free streamer for $2.99 per month. “Howdy was built to make great entertainment affordable, and The Walsh Sisters is a perfect example,” said the streamer’s boss Robin Chacko. “It’s a premium drama with real heart and humor that has already resonated with audiences, critics, and fans of the best-selling book series by Marian Keyes.” Cineflix Rights sells the show and struck the deal. Stephanie Coon, the distrib’s VP of Sales in the Americas, added: “After catching the eyes and hearts of audiences around the globe, we’re thrilled that US viewers will have the chance to fall in love with The Walsh Sisters . Their special blend of family drama, trauma, and humor in the face of it all is the kind of emotional honesty audiences crave.” Kefi Chadwick ( Rivals, Death in Paradise ) wrote two episodes of The Walsh Sisters and the series is directed by Ian Fitzgibbon ( Hullraisers, Moone Boy ). The Walsh Sisters was RTÉ’s highest-rated drama in two years, according to the Irish broadcaster. The Howdy deal was brokered by Elias Patlakas on behalf of Roku. The wider festival program counts 71 films from 38 countries selected from a pool of 1,802 submissions representing 72 countries, with a further eight films screening out of competition. Morning screenings at VOX Cinemas City Centre Al Zahia are reserved for school-aged and university students, while evening screenings are open to the public. Workshops introduce young participants to stop-motion and flipbook animation, alongside workshops on cinematography, production management and content creation. Italy, this year’s country of honor, is represented in the workshop program with “The Italian Eye – Photography Through Light, Color & Composition” and “Tell a Story in Five Shots – Inspired by Italian Cinema.” The festival’s panel lineup turns to what happens once filmmakers have industry-ready work. “Film Festivals Decoded: What Happens After You Press Submit?” brings together festival programmers and directors to discuss the selection process, submissions and how festivals build their programs. University Kuwait executive director of alumni affairs and strategic events Alia Al Azzeh, and Alexandria Short Film Festival head Mohamed Mahmoud. Another panel, “How Do I Get My Next Film Made? From Idea to Financing,” will focus on pitching materials, development labs, producers, financing and co-production opportunities. The festival’s Industry Hub and pitching sessions will run alongside the public program, giving emerging filmmakers opportunities to present projects and connect with industry professionals. title: Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:30am PT Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows By Mya Copeland Plus Icon Mya Copeland Latest Young Audiences Want to Redefine Modern Storytelling, New Study Shows 33 minutes ago ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Screenwriter on Book-to-Screen Changes and Why Jane Austen Is So Adaptable: ‘She’s Almost Like Shakespeare’ 2 days ago Betty McGuire, ‘Growing Pains’ Actress, Dies at 100 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection Begone the days of 30-year-olds playing high schoolers! Gen Z and Gen Alpha want to see themselves depicted accurately on screen. A study from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers at UCLA found that young viewers are often not consulted about what they want to see on screen — even in projects about and for them. Over the past five years, CSS’s annual Teens and Screens Report has worked to change that by providing data about what young people really want to see. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The 2026 report reveals a broad definition of what a “story” is and where to find it, coupled with an appetite for traditional media and in-person experiences. This year’s study surveyed more than 1,500 adolescents aged 10-24. Popular on Variety Among the interesting findings: YouTube (72.9%) ranked as the top medium for storytelling, with nearly four out of five respondents saying that short-term videos can tell a story. 16.8% said they would not cast an influencer in a project, while almost 40% said they would most prefer to cast an unknown actor. Gen Alpha and Gen Z are split on AI: 27.4% of respondents at age 19 identified “doom” as their dominant emotion toward its portrayals in media, while 44.2% of 10 to 13-year-olds described it as “fascinating.” 55% want to see more neurodivergent characters on screen. Friendship is key: 57.3% want to see more platonic relationships represented. “Adults are making stories that they think are going to resonate with young people, but they’re not really talking to a lot of young people to do it,” CSS founder and CEO Yalda T. Uhls, Ph.D., tells Variety about the findings. Uhls is a professor in UCLA’s psychology department who spent nearly two decades as a senior executive at studios like MGM and Sony before pivoting to psychology research of media and young adults. Since launching the Teens and Screens Report, Uhls has seen industry executives and researchers make a concerted effort to integrate the study’s findings. Uhls highlights that individuals from across the industry at CAA, Disney and UTA will attend a summit on Oct. 22 to listen and inform their work. “Our assumptions based on what we thought were stories when we were younger can’t hold,” Uhls says. “They’re not holding, and we need to really talk to young people, do research like this to make sure that these stories are everywhere and they’re consuming it all the time. Make sure that hopefully, if the people we work with that are in the industry — who have the real cultural power, they’re the ones making content that goes all over the world — if they’re really paying attention to our work about what young people need and want and care about, they’re gonna not only probably make content that will resonate and that these young people will see more, but also, it’ll just hopefully create a more empathetic and kind world.” In her work with CSS and the study, Uhls challenges her gut instincts on young people’s take on entertainment. She was surprised to hear participants say they think short-form content like Instagram Reels can tell stories. “So many adults look down on this medium,” Uhls says, but younger audiences “see stories everywhere. They see media. They’re looking for something that they can relate to that resonates with them. And if they don’t see it in a traditional piece of content storytelling in TV, books or movies, they’re going to go elsewhere, and they are going elsewhere.” Uhls describes these young audiences as “way more discerning” than executives might realize. “They like to discover someone new, but yet at the same time, with ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms,’ there’s a different kind of storytelling that’s learned on YouTube really, and maybe TikTok and other things too. So, from a filmmaker perspective, it’s not that they want the stories on those platforms to be translated into mainstream content, but certainly the style and the thinking of their issues and what they do seems to be something Gen Z loves.” But this group Uhls surveys isn’t monolithic, something she stresses is important to remember. She recalls working on her dissertation and realizing that assumptions based only on Los Angeles teens did not ring true across the country. She has two things she hopes executives take away from the study’s findings: “Listening to young people and diverse young people from all over the country is one. And then the second thing is they’re way more nuanced than we give them credit for. They’re way more sophisticated than we give them credit for. Sometimes they say really wise and brilliant things.” CSS will host its sixth annual Teens & Screens Summit on Oct. 22 at the UCLA Meyer and Renee Luskin Conference Center. The event features panels and discussions with industry leaders, researchers and youth activists. Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company Higher Ground Productions will be honored with CSS’s second annual Greg Berlanti Social Impact Award at the event. title: Disney and Netflix Are Courting Creators. YouTube Is Playing Hardball to Keep Them
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 21, 2026 6:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Texas-based sports creators Dude Perfect inked a wide-ranging partnership with Disney that will span entertainment, sports, consumer products and experiences. Illustrated by Neil Jamieson On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the video platform has been cooking up in its Skunk Works, like new AI video editing tools. But this year, YouTube wasn’t the only platform on their minds. Netflix, Disney+, Tubi and others are aggressively cutting deals for top creators, in some cases securing wholly original programming or day-and-date releases with YouTube, offering millions of dollars in the process. The Google-owned video platform is not taking it lying down, launching a carrot-and-stick approach to try and keep its place as the primary home for top talent. “It’s a very good time to be in the creator business,” says Adam Wescott, CEO of Home Game Studios, noting the demand for their work. With creator-owned studios proliferating nationwide, it’s a battle that could portend the future of streaming entertainment. It started with kids and family content. Netflix, seeking to bolster its kids programming, inked deals for YouTube native content from CoComelon , Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober. It worked, with all three becoming among the most watched programs in the category. The streamer subsequently ordered originals from them and began to reach out to creators in other genres, spanning food (Nick DiGiovanni), talk ( Good Mythical Morning with Rhett & Link) and teen content (Alan Chikin Chow). Rich Greenfield, the LightShed analyst, believes Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion on creator and podcast programming over the next three years (still, admittedly, a very small slice of its $20 billion annual content budget). But Netflix only started the current war. Disney has long worked with creators, but recent months have seen wide-ranging deals with the likes of Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect and Like Nastya as it seeks out family-friendly and on-brand creators who can live on Disney+. And the company recently hosted a creator event at the El Capitan Theater and Disney Studios Lot, with some 350 creators to further forge those relationships. Tubi, the Fox-owned streaming service, has inked deals with dozens of creators for both originals and library fare. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Dhar Mann at YouTube Brandcast at David Geffen Hall on May 14, 2025 in New York City. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for YouTube There’s already hope in the creator community that Skydance is about to follow them, with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz having served as the CEO of Maker Studios. But why are these other streamers so eager to get in the creator business? Multiple sources paint a picture built around audience, money and speed. The larger studio platforms and streamers desperately want to have a product that appeals to the younger, digitally native audience that religiously watches creator content on YouTube. “I think creators really do value, in the right circumstances, the elevation and amplification of being on a main channel platform like a traditional media company,” says Akshay Mehta, the CEO of Lighthouse Studios, a creator entertainment studio. “Creators are creatives fundamentally. They just discovered that in the last 15 years, for a lot of people, the best way to be creative is to go make stuff on YouTube.” The money certainly helps. Multiple sources on the creator side stress that they need funding to help pursue some of the ideas they have, and such places as Netflix, Tubi and Disney are helping them do that. The big streamers are funding original shows and offering help to break into areas like consumer products or live experiences (that was a key piece of Disney’s Dude Perfect deal). Streamers also are banking that creators can not only bring their audience with them but fill their libraries with content that is, frankly, dramatically less expensive than traditional fare and that is produced at a more rapid clip. “These platforms have seen this shift, and they can’t ignore it,” says Nic Paul, the president of the creator services company Spotter. “They all have subscriptions, they all have ad-supported products, even at Netflix, the ad-supported product is becoming a lot more of the focus. There’s a lot of churn. Everyone is like, how do I create enough content fast to keep audiences engaged? Because if you think about it, Stranger Things on Netflix, I’ve got to wait a year plus for a season, and creators are obviously very fast at putting out IP.” Indeed, one top creator who has a deal with a streaming platform says they told their new partner that they can produce an hour’s worth of programming at perhaps 10 percent of the cost (or less!) of a traditional comedy, drama or unscripted concept, all at a faster pace. But what has surprised creators more than anything is how hard YouTube is fighting back. The platform is a juggernaut, and it would be just fine if it lost top creators to other places. But it is waging a multipronged effort — with both incentives and threats — to try and convince creators to make YouTube their primary home. Many of the incentives focus on brand deals, with YouTube significantly increasing its resources in the space. Some creators see YouTube’s brand deals as a way to subsidize or pay for content that they want to make, given that YouTube does not pay to license content in the same way platforms like Netflix do. “Given the cultural phenomenon that YouTube creators are, and this sort of juggernaut that they are in the culture out there, of course other streaming platform services have taken note,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told the Big Technology podcast after Made on YouTube when pressed on the dispute, adding that even as MrBeast produces his Beast Games for Prime Video, he still keeps YouTube as his home base. “And, frankly, I think that’s flattering to our creators.” But YouTube also has played hardball, with one creator telling THR that they were “shocked” at the platform’s approach. On the one hand, some of the threats are reasonable: YouTube selects a handful of creators to appear onstage at its annual Brandcast upfront event, a high-profile stage that can lead to major deals. And it has supported Emmy campaigns for creators in certain categories. Those would stop for creators who shift their allegiances to other platforms. (Netflix and Disney already have promised to bring creators to their own upfronts next year and fund some Emmy efforts, according to sources.) And they have even suggested that creators may not be eligible for YouTube Select, an ad program for its very top creators. That caught some creators off guard, as it was seen as an objective program based on reach and scale and is built around videos on YouTube. “That was never their approach in the past,” says Wescott. “It was always about supporting creators and reminding them why YouTube was their home.” Lilly Singh has spoken out candidly about the difference between working in the traditional Hollywood system vs. the creator-driven YouTube economy. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images The platform still plays that game, though even there the tone has become somewhat combative, as one creator notes to THR . Earlier in October, comedian Lilly Singh returned to YouTube after a years-long hiatus, once again creating original content after working in Hollywood. In an interview YouTube posted to its blog , she did not hold back. “Hollywood has real systemic issues, especially for women and people of color. Over the past few years, I received countless notes that weren’t about improving the project, but about making it ‘more palatable,” ‘more marketable,’ or ‘less niche.’ That is fundamentally anti-creative. Our job is to tell our stories unapologetically,” Singh said. “On YouTube, there are no gatekeepers demanding I make my brain baby more palatable for the masses. That authenticity is why my channel worked in the first place.” Message received. But why is YouTube seem so interested in keeping creators on-platform? Especially because, as Mohan notes, it’s a good thing for the ecosystem when others are interested? “On the surface, YouTube should not care. Creators are not launching their careers on Netflix or Disney+,” LightShed analyst Greenfield wrote on Oct. 9. “We suspect YouTube is concerned because the top 20-50 creators have an outsized importance to its major brand advertising commitments each year. Most brands only know a select group of high-profile creators. If brands start to see those creators appearing on Netflix… does a brand start to ask why it is paying YouTube for creators it can find in a curated, brand-safe environment elsewhere?” Advertising is at the heart of the battle, with the ad-supported Tubi competing with Netflix and Disney (each of which is leaning into ads) for creator deals. Creators, of course, are used to working with brands. “A dirty little secret of our space is 90 percent of the revenue is brand endorsements, influencer marketing,” Wescott notes. Still, none of the creators (or those who worked with top creators) suggest that they will completely leave YouTube, even if they may still cut deals to develop original ideas elsewhere. And it isn’t just out of loyalty to the platform that made them or that funds them (Instagram and TikTok, they note, pay basically nothing). “I think you’ll be hard pressed to find a successful YouTube creator who’s willing to walk away from that platform, because it’s what they know, it’s where their audience is, it’s where they grew their business, and it’s where they have the most direct control,” says Wescott. “You’re still playing on someone else’s playground, but YouTube is not telling you what to post on your channel. The other guys are going to have some sort of opinion on what you create on the original side.” For an ambitious creator, it may mean taking a more strategic approach to how, when, and where they choose to produce content. “I’m distributing on [YouTube], I’m paying for everything, I’m getting paid, which is amazing, but now I’ve got to start thinking like a CEO and be like, wait, hold on, strategically, what is my distribution? Where is my next thing coming from?” says Paul. It’s a question that will be felt across the entertainment world. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Interscope Unveils Exec Promotions Following Shake Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All October 21, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle An, Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle. courtesy of Interscope Interscope revealed a suite of promotions on Tuesday, a week after the record label and parent company Universal Music Group underwent a round of layoffs and executive departures as part of UMG’s previously-announced cost-savings measure that started in 2024. Longtime Interscope exec Michelle An has been named president and Chief Creative Officer at the label, Interscope said, adding that An would both IGA’s pop/rock division as well as have a broader role across the whole roster to help artists “shape the worlds around their music, from visual identity and storytelling to brand development and long-term career strategy.” “IGA has always been defined by original voices and by the teams who back those voices with taste, conviction and care,” John Janick, Chairman and CEO of Interscope Capitol, said in a statement. “Michelle has one of the clearest creative instincts in the business. She helps artists make the world around their music feel bold, fully realized and unmistakably their own.” Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle, meanwhile, have been named co-presidents of Urban at the label. The two are well-respected hip-hop marketing executives, and Interscope said the duo “will bring A&R, marketing innovation, digital strategy and audience development closer together for IGA Urban’s artists.” “Laura and Ramon bring complementary strengths to IGA Urban,” Janick said. “Laura has earned deep trust through her artist relationships, creative judgment and commitment to developing talent. Ramon brings cultural instinct, deep digital expertise and a sharp understanding of how artists build audiences and communities. Together, they will connect A&R, marketing and digital strategy around each artist’s vision, helping IGA Urban artists move with more clarity, momentum, and impact.” Interscope’s pop/rock and urban divisions were impacted by last week’s restructuring as Sam Riback, Interscope’s co-president and head of pop/rock A&R, as well as Nicole Wyskoarko, the label’s head of urban A&R, both departed.
