title: Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G
full_text: Skip to main content Sacha Baron Cohen was photographed Oct. 14 at PMC Studios Los Angeles. Styling by Artistic & Fashion Director Alison Edmond Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? , is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose their prejudices, and he’s even more tired of the death threats that periodically follow. There are easier ways to make money in this business, and eventually his luck will run out. The trouble with his declaration, however impassioned, is that he has been making it for years. He’d routinely say he was done before he made the 2020 Borat sequel, which, incidentally, earned two Oscar nominations, and he was even more insistent afterward. And each time he says it, he believes it to be true. He wants it to be true, he tells me. So, why are we here, I ask, discussing an Ali G revival? “Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy,” he says. “I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence.” There’s a level of seriousness that belies the 90-minute comedy film he’s made, which features an imbecilic white rapper who speaks in Caribbean-British slang and a contraption that shoots bullets out of one’s rear end. Recognizing this, he adds: “And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made.” His longtime collaborators have other theories about his return. Anthony “Ant” Hines, who’s been working with Baron Cohen since The 11 O’Clock Show , where the Ali G character originated, believes his pal had missed the adrenaline rush, just as he had. “It’s a visceral buzz you get from making a movie this way,” Hines says, “and nothing comes close to it.” Dan Mazer, whose friendship with Baron Cohen dates back to secondary school in the U.K., wasn’t particularly surprised to get the call about dusting off Ali G, in part because they’ve never stopped talking about the character. In fact, whenever they got together, they’d often slip into Ali G’s voice, he says, and imagine what patently absurd things he would be saying or doing in different situations. “I also think it’s a knowledge that Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this sort of filmmaking,” says Mazer. “And yeah, Michael Jordan went off and tried to play baseball, and you go, ‘OK, you’re a pretty good baseball player,’ but he’s not the Michael Jordan of baseball. And Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this, and to an extent, we all are. We invented this genre, and nobody else has matched what we’ve done.” Whatever the reasoning may be, Ali G is back, rolling into theaters Oct. 23 before landing on Amazon Prime Video soon after. And like plenty else that Baron Cohen has done, it’s already prompted a full-blown meta-outrage cycle, complete with a campaign to boycott the film. With each new trailer or PR stunt posted to social media come fresh accusations of an outdated caricature and of cultural appropriation — the latter a central plot point in the film, in which Ali G’s progressive nemesis (also played by Baron Cohen) attempts to cancel him on those very grounds. Some in his camp have speculated that it’s more of a coordinated attack by pro-Palestinians who are critical of Baron Cohen’s past support of Israel. (Though he’s been quiet about Israeli politics and the conflict in Gaza in recent years, Baron Cohen is a prominent Jew who has sounded the alarm about the surge of antisemitism on social media, reportedly telling TikTok executives in 2023 that what was happening on their platform was “creating the biggest antisemitic movement since the Nazis.”) Colton Dunn, an Emmy-winning Ali G superfan and one of three Black writers hired on the film, is aware of the cultural appropriation claims. “But we knew where we were coming from, and we dealt with it all in the movie,” he says, “and at the heart of it, Sacha and the movie want to defeat evil and hate. That’s the intention behind it.” Still, the internet has suggested the backlash has Amazon spooked. Courtenay Valenti, Amazon MGM Studios’ head of film, streaming and theatrical, offers this: “We want to be in business with exceptional storytellers who have distinctive creative visions, and Sacha is exactly that. He has always been fearless in his comedy, with a unique ability to tap into the cultural conversation in ways that are both provocative and entertaining.” Over cappuccinos in the garden of the Chateau Marmont, Baron Cohen lets loose on the mounting backlash, his battles with studios and the $3 million day that nearly derailed his film. Paul Smith robe; Wander socks; stylist’s own slippers; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses, hat. Photographed By Beau Grealy In 2021, you allegedly performed as Ali G at The Comedy Store in Australia. How soon after did you explore the idea of another film, and what did those early conversations entail? During the pandemic, our family moves to Australia, and when they lock down in Australia, you cannot leave where you are. My ex [Isla Fisher] is from Perth, so we applied to go there. She’s rejected. I find out that you have to show that there’s a financial benefit to Western Australia to be allowed in. You have to apply to the police. So I say, “Listen, I’m doing a stand-up tour. It’s going to create 300 jobs. It’s going to bring tens of millions of dollars into Western Australia.” Obviously I had no intention of doing it. But then the police accept me. We spent 14 days in lockdown, and at the end, a police car turns up, an inspector comes out, and she says, “I am in charge of your stand-up tour.” So, you had to do a stand-up tour. I did, and I had the police watching me. I ended up doing a 90-minute show, and what was interesting was that people really loved seeing Borat and Bruno, but when Ali G came out, there was a different response. It was as if people believed he was real. There’s going to be a lot of amateur psychology in this interview, but my observation was that because Ali G existed before I existed as a public figure — for five or six years, I didn’t give an interview [as myself] — people thought Ali was real and therefore there was this different response to him. So, I felt, “Hold on, is there a movie in this character?” I came back to America at the end of 2021 and started talking with the team about it. We all felt Ali by himself wouldn’t be a satirical movie because he was from a bygone era — this relic from another period who’s unaware that he is deeply problematic. But what if we brought in another character, an ultraprogressive extremist [also played by Baron Cohen] who’s his rival and make it a thriller like The Fugitive ? We had in our mind this line that goes, “We have a cultural appropriator on the loose,” from that famous speech in The Fugitive . That felt funny to me. In the revisionist history of the film, you had ended Da Ali G Show because you couldn’t come to financial terms with HBO. It left me wondering if there were any conversations or interest, from either side, about doing more? Oh, yes. HBO wanted to carry on. I said no because at that time, in Britain, I think a lot of comedians were snobs about doing multiple seasons. So, there was no expectation or desire to do 15 seasons — to do the American way. I’m very friendly with Larry David, and I’m jealous of him that he can do Curb again and again. I probably would’ve had a much easier life if I just carried on doing Da Ali G Show . Paul Smith sweater, pants; Wander socks; Doucal’s boots; Ali G’s own jewelry, glasses. A decade ago, you said of this type of filmmaking: “It’s a young man’s game. You have to be prepared for a small amount of risk, and my philosophy was always: ‘Well, if something bad happens, I’m single and everyone’s going to be all right if I end up in hospital for two weeks.’ Now that I’m married with kids, it’s more difficult to justify.” So, did you find a way to do it differently, or did you just say, “Fuck it”? I’m never cavalier. These movies are dangerous to make, but we try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe. But even physically, they’re incredibly demanding. So, the final scene of this film is an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations. It’s a continual shot. There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert. On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, “You will go to hospital if you make this movie,” because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, “You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.” You hear that and think what? That I have to fix the problem. So, I had an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France be by my side during the scene and they’re measuring my weight. I think I had 11 liters of Pedialyte. And listen, a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration, including the bodyguard. There were dangers in the scene as well. One of the people grabbed a gun and almost did something very dangerous. These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI. If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy. As I read your own quote back to you just now, you were laughing. Why? Because I’m always surprised at my own idiocy. I’m very bad at looking into the future and imagining how I will feel. So, for example, the naked fight in Borat 1 , we get to set and Ken Davitian, who’s not conventionally attractive, is naked, and he’s going to sit on my face. And I say, “I’m not going to do this!” At that point, Larry Charles, the director, said, “So why did you write it?!” I continually make these decisions that are very bad for my own health and sanity. You are making this film in a very different moment, culturally and comedically. Do you derive some masochistic pleasure from that kind of challenge? I’ll tell you, in the script, there was a moment where Ali G is canceled, and the way we wanted to do that was that I, Sacha, should be canceled in the real world and the idea was to use the footage of me being canceled and stick it into the movie. And we did actually get some of the second bit, but we didn’t have the money to open up the movie and put the footage in. That was the intention, though. I’m told you get a fair number of death threats, which now come from both the left and the right. When have you decided something wasn’t worth it? I was about to do a scene [in Borat 1 ] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, “Why is your gun on your thigh?” He goes, “Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.” I said, “Well, how close are you to me?” And he said, “I’ll be with you within three minutes.” I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene. I will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die. Thom Sweeney shirt; Ali G’s ring, sunglasses. Photographed By Beau Grealy You’ve filmed in a bulletproof vest, so you’ve clearly anticipated the possibility of being shot? Yes, on Borat 2 , there was a scene at a gun rights rally that I knew there was a risk of getting shot. But I felt it was an important film to be made. Is there anyone who says to you, “Hey, Sacha, I know this seems noble to you, but maybe it’s not necessary”? Yes. Who? Your children? I don’t talk about my children. But my brothers tell me that. And my mom and some of my team as well, because there are much easier options. I made a movie called Ladies First . I shot it in three months. It came out. A lot of people saw it [on Netflix]. And it’s as financially beneficial as making something that takes years, and there’s absolutely zero risk. There must be some masochistic nature to me, but I don’t think it’s just that. I want to give the fans who’ve been loyal for the last 28 years something that they’ve never seen before. I want to give them the most ambitious movie I’ve ever made, which is a three-character movie. [Baron Cohen also plays a former Mossad agent.] It is my version of the Avengers. I’ve always assumed that you were like Tom Cruise, after the same adrenaline rush that he is as he jumps out of planes. I don’t think that’s the reason I do it. You don’t? Your collaborators seem to … No. The first [for-hire] movie I did, Talladega Nights , I walked into my trailer and there was a bed there. I realized I’d never been in a trailer before, and I go, “Hold on, this is a paid job where I can go to sleep?!” I couldn’t comprehend how relatively easy it was, and it was great fun. But as you’ll probably deduce from this interview, I’m not very self-aware. Paul Smith sweater; Ali G’s jewelry. Photographed By Beau Grealy I don’t know that I buy that. OK. Do I enjoy it when something works? Yes. Am I upset when something doesn’t work? Yes. So, for example, this final scene is an eight-hour continuous shot over multiple locations and no one had ever done that before. Normally we shoot a scene or two scenes a day. Here, we put probably 40 scenes together and shot them continuously. I had a variety of line producers and assistant directors refuse to schedule it. And there are 400 or so beats that must all go perfectly, because you’re dealing with real people and if anything doesn’t feel quite right, they will stop and say, “Hold on, this isn’t real.” Of course. So gunfire, the squibs have to go off perfectly. A medical procedure happens. That body that we use has to be believable. Then a fire breaks out during the first part of the scene. As we’re driving to the second location to kidnap somebody with these real people, I find out that location four is surrounded by fire, and it’s being evacuated, and we have to pull the scene. And each time we run it, it’s $4 million and we’re insured for $1 million, and I personally have to pay $3 million. So, we shut down production and we have a discussion, which is that it’s completely idiotic that we’re trying this. And everyone is telling you it’s not possible? Yes, and I’ve lost $3 million that day. Obviously it was my money, which is a very stupid idea. But you ultimately got it? We got it. We had some of the team that worked on the Oscars because I was like, “What is a movie or a TV show where nothing can go wrong? It’s the Oscars.” And even there, sometimes something’s going wrong! I said to them, “OK, this is the Oscars, it’s just taking place over 50 miles in 12 locations. And it has gunfire and blood.” But at the end of all of it, if you look at the behind-the-scenes footage, I’m not jumping up and down. I’m content. The Ali G film, which has Baron Cohen playing three different characters, suffered multiple shutdowns and a change of studios. Michael Legato © 2026 Amazon Content Services With 2020’s Borat 2 , you’ve said that several of the places you pitched were concerned by the political content and the idea of running it before the election. How did this pitch compare? Well, the desire was always to have this come out a few days before either a presidential election or the midterms. A lot of my movies have come out around those times. Borat 1 came out almost 20 years to the day, on November 3, 2006, just before the midterms. It’s a time for people to think about the choices that they’re about to make. But this movie is more about the dangers of extremism on both sides. I get that, but you’re also operating in an extremely risk-averse climate. I can’t imagine there weren’t any concerns … Well, Hollywood is a superficial place. Noooo. I know. ( Laughter. ) But I pitched this after Borat 2 had won two Golden Globes and had Oscar nominations and was the most watched movie ever on Amazon. That’s enough to convince studio heads to buy it. And everyone tried. It was somewhere else first, no? Yes. Amazon and Universal were the final contenders. We ended up going with Universal but, in the end, the movie took so long that we went back to Amazon. And it was actually great because we’d had an incredible experience there with the last one. We really did. And that movie [ Borat 2 ] also was at Universal and ended up at Amazon. So, this one moved because — It was taking too long. You have to understand the basis of this kind of movie is that we have to find people who don’t know who I am, which becomes harder and harder. I think our research department interviewed 5,000 doctors to get one [for a single scene]. Then we had a number of other things that kept on shutting it down. The fire. The writers strike. I ended up doing another movie in the middle. Baron Cohen was joined by 300 Ali G look-alikes who followed him around London for a viral promo stunt Oct. 11. Jeff Spicer/Getty Images Amazon came aboard a third of the way through. What did their notes look like? For better or worse, maybe for worse, I’m a final-cut producer and director. So, you’re saying it didn’t much matter what their notes were? Well, executives can have really fantastic notes. And they can have terrible notes. But I always listen to the audience and I’m really guided by that. You were once asked about comparisons between you and Andy Kaufman, to which you said, “In a way, he’s more of an artist than I am in that I don’t think he cared what the audience thought — and deep down, I really want to make the audience laugh. And that’s why I fight to get jokes to be funny … I’ll go to war with whatever studio has been stupid enough to pay me money to make a movie.” Again, you’re laughing … I can’t believe how honest I was. What did those fights look like on a film like this? If something is funny, then I will go to war for it. And the studios know that because I make it clear when we do these movies, which makes me not very studio-friendly in some ways because my allegiance is to the audience. And I go to every single screening and I record the laughter and I grade the jokes and I have a few people that I’ve trained to grade them too, and then I cut the jokes within a frame. It’s obsessive and very intricate, but it’s designed to deliver really funny movies. Some people find me incredibly arrogant because they’ll come up and say, “You know that movie, Borat 2 , wasn’t funny.” And I’ll say, “You’re entitled to your opinion, but you’re wrong. I have 5,000 people laughing at these jokes and I can show you they are empirically funny.” While the vast majority of the Ali G cast are unsuspecting nonactors, Baron Cohen and his onscreen partner, played by Morgana Robinson, are the exceptions. Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios You said that you’re not studio-friendly, but, as you noted, this is a superficial business and if your model can put butts in seats … Yes, it’s about money. But I’m also a great supporter of the Oscars and other awards ceremonies because, however absurd they are, it creates another incentive for studio heads to make quality projects. Because studio heads do want to win Oscars and they want to get nominated. And we’ve been very lucky in that the Academy and the Globes and some other organizations have recognized our work. In fact, I was sitting at that table [pointing to another table in the Chateau garden] in 2006 having done Borat , and Sean Penn came and sat at the table and he said, “Why don’t you do an Oscar campaign for your performance in Borat ?” I said, “That’s absurd. They’ll never give me an Oscar nomination.” And he said, “They will.” So, we went to Fox at the time and they said, “Listen, we’ll pay for one Oscar campaign, but it’s either writing or acting.” At the time, I was actually winning some of the acting awards, to my great surprise, but I spoke to the team and we decided to push the writing. [The 2006 film was nominated for best adapted screenplay.] So, we gave up the acting campaign. Also, I was about to make Bruno and I didn’t want to go on a baby-kissing tour, which would destroy my next movie. Me doing this kind of stuff [an interview as himself] destroys the ability to make another one. I know, I know. I’m sorry. There we go. Look what you’ve done. You’ve ruined me. As you anticipated, it didn’t take long for people to start lodging complaints. One criticism, which mirrors a plotline in the film, is that Ali G uses the character as a cover for enforcing racial stereotypes. What do you say to that? Well, I’ll repeat what I’ve said for many years, which is that Ali G is a white cultural appropriator who steals from the musical artists that he admires. The reason Ali G says “West Side” is not because the Afro-Caribbean community in London was saying “West Side.” Nobody there was. It’s because Tupac Shakur, who he admires, is saying “West Side.” And so he is funny because he is delusional. He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton, and that is the absurdity of Ali G. The core joke is that a white moron, possibly the stupidest man in the world, is interviewing a white expert or high-status politician, and that white expert or high-status politician believes that this imbecile played by me is real and that leads to comedy. And in my belief, it slightly undermines the power of the establishment. So it was fundamentally an anti-establishment character where we’re pricking the assuredness of the establishment by saying, “Listen, these people aren’t that smart. They believe that Channel 4 or HBO could have sent one of the most stupid people in the world to interview them.” Baron Cohen as Bruno in 2009 in Berlin. Sean Gallup/Getty Images What do you make of the argument that not everybody recognizes the absurdity and so the stereotypes being presented can have dangerous ramifications? Everyone is entitled to their own view. And a lot of the stuff on social media is orchestrated, and not necessarily orchestrated by people who really believe in what they’re saying. We’ll get to that. But when I did Da Ali G Show in America, the first people who gravitated to it were the Black hip-hop community. The first GQ Award that I was given was given to me by Method Man and Redman. I did a series of adverts for the NBA directed by Spike Lee, who’s not naive about racial issues. They recognized these characters, these white cultural appropriators, and they found them funny. So, this notion of it being problematic hadn’t been raised for 20 years. OK, but you seemed to know it would be this time around? Yes. I knew, and I wanted to make sure that this was an anti-racist movie, which is why we were so concerned with having absolutely brilliant Black writers on board and consulting with brilliant Black cultural commentators. As I believe you were referencing, there was a pretty sizable social media campaign to boycott the movie, and some have speculated that the campaign is tied to your pro-Israel stance — Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel. [Baron Cohen voiced his support for Israel and the hostages immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks but has been quiet on the Gaza war and Israeli politics in the years since.] I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix. For example, I co-founded a group called Stop Hate for Profit with the NAACP and Color of Change and the ADL and certain other civil rights groups to stop the misinformation and incitement of racism on social media. So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced. You’ve been vocal about the rise of antisemitism, broadly speaking. Have you felt any difference in your own Hollywood career after Oct. 7? No, not really. I mean, maybe it’s because I don’t do much, but I haven’t. Well, you’re about to make your West End debut in a Quentin Tarantino play, which feels like a big leap, going from this film, in which you’re in complete control as the writer, director and star, to being a puppet in Tarantino’s theater. How did that come together? I’ve never had a career plan, but I have this kind of no-brainer rule, which is if one of the best directors in the world asks me to do something, I’ll say yes, even if it’s instinctively the wrong project. So when Martin Scorsese says, “I’m doing a kid’s film, will Sacha play the villain in it?” And I read the book and the character’s not that interesting. I actually had a lot of arguments with [screenwriter John] Logan about it [ Hugo ]. But I say yes because I want to learn how to make better films. And so if Quentin comes along and says, “I want to do a play,” I say yes. Then I actually read the play and I thought it was fantastic. And I felt, why not? So currently, I’m doing nine hours of sword-fighting training a week. And I would just clarify, rather than be a puppet, Quentin did suggest that there would be some element of collaboration. As Borat, sporting a mankini in Cannes in 2006. Anthony Harvey – PA Images/PA Images via Getty Images Have you seen it yet? A little bit, yes. But Quentin and I have been talking about doing a project for at least 20 years. We talked about doing The Scarlet Pimpernel about 20 years ago. Borat came out and Quentin and I would have dinner monthly and I almost did a part in [his 2012 Western] Django Unchained . In the end, I had to drop out because I ended up doing Les Misérables . But I came very close to doing a scene with Kerry Washington. I even had a prosthetic chin made because Quentin was very adamant that I would resemble this character he’d liked from the ’40s. Ant Hines, one of your longtime collaborators, suggested you’ve tussled with Amazon in the promotion of this new film. “We’re giving Amazon panic attacks on the daily,” he told me. “They’re used to Timothée Chalamet eating some chicken wings; they’re not used to 300 Timothée Chalamets attempting to take part in the London Marathon, which is a thing they shut down.” This is why it’s best not to talk to somebody like Ant. ( Laughs. ) You know, they’ve actually been great in terms of the marketing. But it’s not a traditional process when you work with me and you’re marketing a movie. You did end up with 300 Ali G look-alikes following you around London. That had to be validating, if a little overwhelming. The really concerning thing was that these fans were coming out with catchphrases that I’d completely forgotten. I was like, “Wait a minute. I recognize that … What is that from?” And they’d go, “It’s you!” And some of them were doing better Ali G impressions than me. There was one guy there, an Ali G impersonator, and I had to explain, like, “Listen, you’ve been doing this at weddings and bar mitzvahs every week for the last 20 years. I haven’t been doing this.” I’ve actually had that happen before. We did a movie called Bruno , and Jonah Hill was one of the writers. And in the writers room, he was doing impressions of Bruno, and they were better than Bruno. Then when I started shooting the movie, I realized that I was doing an impression of Jonah Hill doing an impression of me. In any genre, there’s always an “It” person, and at various points, you’ve employed those people shortly before they reached that status: Jonah, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and, most recently, Nathan Fielder, who worked on your Showtime series, Who Is America? What do you think of what Nathan has done in the eight years since you worked together? Oh, I think he’s a comic genius and he reinvented the genre that I, I suppose, created or developed. And he had a rule, really, which was to not do anything that I had done. But he’s a brilliant, brilliant mind, and absolutely hilarious. I think his documentary [ You Can See Everything ] is going to be huge, so I’m very excited for him. But it’s been an honor to have all of these incredible people come and work with me. Seth and Evan, the story with them was, it was the Ali G Show , and they came in with an idea for Bruno — instead of Girls Gone Wild , it was Boys Gone Wild . I said, “OK, you’re hired, but I’ve only got enough money for one writer, so unless you want to share a hotel room and a bed and a wage, I can only hire one of you and it’s going to be Seth.” They came back and said, “We’ll split the wage.” And basically they would write in a double bed in the Best Western hotel we were in. They had beers all around them. They were smoking and they’d write in bed. That’s fantastic. For you, what do the incoming calls look like these days? I think they’re kind of what comes in to everyone. I get the traditional comedies, kernels of comedy ideas, and then dramas. Is one genre more appealing than the other right now? No. I want to do stuff that challenges me. So again, I’m not doing Borat 3 , which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more. Until the next one … No, no, I really have had enough. I know you don’t believe me. I do not. Oh, I really pray that in six years’ time, you don’t come to me and quote me to myself. This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: Neiman Marcus’s Luxe 2026 Holiday Offerings Include $180,000 ‘Star Wars’ Experience
full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. For “ Star Wars ” fans with $180,000 to spare, Neiman Marcus is offering something even harder to come by than a vintage lightsaber: a look inside the famously guarded world of Lucasfilm. The luxury department store has unveiled its annual Fantasy Gifts collection , headlined by a one-of-a-kind “Star Wars” experience that includes private access to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, custom lightsabers and four VIP tickets to an upcoming “Star Wars” world premiere and afterparty. The six-figure package arrives ahead of the franchise’s 50th anniversary in 2027, when Disney and Lucasfilm will release Shawn Levy’s highly anticipated “Star Wars: Starfighter.” Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately Des Willie The experience begins at One Letterman in San Francisco’s Presidio, home to Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, the visual effects company George Lucas founded in 1975. Guests will receive private, behind-the-scenes access to the studios where some of Hollywood’s most recognizable cinematic worlds have been brought to life, along with a visit to an active Lucasfilm production. Also included is a one-of-one replica of an “Ahsoka” Season 2 lightsaber hilt prop signed by Lucasfilm president and chief creative officer Dave Filoni, as well as a private consultation to design a pair of custom-assembled lightsabers. The experience culminates in four VIP tickets to an upcoming Star Wars world premiere and afterparty, offering the opportunity to celebrate alongside the franchise’s cast and creators. Lucasfilm also prepares to celebrate half a century since the release of George Lucas’s original 1977 film. The anniversary comes amid a new theatrical chapter for the franchise, with “The Mandalorian & Grogu” slated for May 2026 and Levy’s “Starfighter,” starring Ryan Gosling, set to arrive in theaters in May 2027. The “Star Wars” package is the centerpiece of Neiman Marcus’ 2026 Holiday Book, which is celebrating its own milestone: 100 years since the retailer introduced its now-famous holiday catalog. This year’s edition, titled “Grand Gestures,” continues the Fantasy Gifts tradition that began in 1959, when Stanley Marcus started offering customers elaborate, sometimes outrageous presents that money could buy — provided they had enough of it. And while a $180,000 trip inside the “Star Wars” universe may be the most obvious draw for Hollywood obsessives, the rest of this year’s lineup is similarly ambitious. For fashion and jewelry collectors, Neiman Marcus is offering a six-day trip through Venice, Florence and Milan hosted by the Buccellati family, featuring private museum and atelier visits and a design session with Andrea Buccellati to create a bespoke piece of high jewelry. Another package, offered in partnership with Verdura, takes guests to New York City for a private tour of the jeweler’s historical collection and a fitting for a custom Maltese Cross cuff set with emeralds, sapphires and diamonds, followed by dinner at Orso and producer house seats to a Broadway show. Dolce & Gabbana is contributing a Carretto Siciliano foosball table, complete with hand-painted Sicilian artwork, solid wood construction and a screen-printed glass playing field. A fragrance experience with Saujet and Lalique includes a trip to Alsace, France, where guests will stay at Villa René Lalique, participate in a perfume masterclass and receive an exclusive first-edition crystal fragrance trunk. For those who prefer being on the water, another gift includes a fully loaded electric Arc Sport wake boat, personalized equipment and private lessons with world champion wakesurfer Austin Keen. And in perhaps the most sentimental offering of the bunch, customers can work with Neiman Marcus’ corporate chef to refine a cherished family recipe, which will then appear on the retailer’s restaurant menus nationwide for a full year. “The 2026 Fantasy Gifts continue to redefine extraordinary luxury through one-in-a-lifetime experiences, unparalleled access, and boundless imagination,” Darcy Penick, president and chief commercial officer of Exemplar Luxury Group, Neiman Marcus’ parent company, said in a statement. This year’s holiday campaign, dubbed “Holiday Fantasy,” also features supermodel Natasha Poly in imagery shot by director and photographer Alexandre Bassard at Neiman Marcus’ Beverly Hills store. The retailer is rolling out additional in-store events, holiday dining experiences and gift guides across its locations and digital channels. A portion of every Fantasy Gift purchase will benefit the Heart of Neiman Marcus Foundation through a corporate donation. The retailer is also continuing its seasonal fundraising campaign for Boys & Girls Clubs of America. Loading comments...

title: Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 6:00am PT Jake Tapper Sketches Work Outside CNN: Graphic Novel Probes Life of ‘Butcher’ Klaus Barbie By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Starz Gets Back on Verizon Fios After New Carriage Pact 20 hours ago Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon’s Prime Video 23 hours ago Meet Kate DePetro, Fox News’ Social-Media Ambassador to Younger Viewers 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Top Shelf/Elliott O'Donovan Many of the stories, interviews and analyses Jake Tapper presents to his followers on CNN rely heavily on moving pictures, courtesy of his employer. A new project from the anchor and author will substitute still images — that Tapper drew himself. Tapper has spent the past three years working on a graphic novel, and much of his time was spent drawing every panel. “ The Butcher : The Decades-Long Hunt for Klaus Barbie, One of the World’s Most Notorious Killers,” will publish on June 1, 2027, from Top Shelf Productions. The illustrated novel examines the story of Klaus Barbie, the Nazi figure known as the “Butcher of Lyon” who escaped Germany and avoided capture for decades, until Nazi hunters and journalists tracked him down. Tapper, who first became interested in the story while visiting France with his family, used source material in four different languages to chronicle the pursuit for Barbie in excruciating detail. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately “It’s just this fascinating story about this young Nazi who comes to Leon, France, terrorizes the city, and then pops up years later in South America in Bolivia,” says the CNN anchor during a recent interview. “He also helped support a right-wing government in South America before eventually being captured.” In what may be a surprising twist, the journalist presents eyebrow-raising information about who helped Barbie escape Europe. Popular on Variety Graphic novels are a favored medium of younger readers who not only read coming-of-age tales or longer stories involving fictional characters, but also memoirs that deeply probe cultures or perspectives that may not turn up in more mainstream media formats. Top Shelf, Tapper’s publisher, has released graphic novels such as “From Hell” by Alan Moore and Eddie Campbell, “They Called Us Enemy” by actor George Takei, and the “March” trilogy co-written by Congressman John Lewis. Tapper may best be known for anchoring “The Lead” and “ State of the Union ” on CNN as well as some special news events, but he has long juggled his news job with a suite of other activities. He has written eight books, including three novels. What people may not know about him is that he has been drawn to comics and cartooning for most of his life. As a child, he avidly read Charles Schulz’ “Peanuts” and Walt Kelly’s “Pogo,” as well as super-heroes like Batman and Superman. His home office contains strips of “Little Orphan Annie,” “Doonesbury” and “Zippy the Pinhead.” Some of his work has been seen in Roll Call, the college paper at Dartmouth when he attended, and even in a local paper, The South Street Star, where he grew up. For a period of time, he drew a fresh piece for CNN’s “State of the Union” “It’s a very American art form,” he says of the medium. “There’s just a brilliance. It’s not filmed, but it’s not written. It’s somewhere in between.” Still, CNN viewers haven’t seen the end-of-show political cartoons he once drew in several years. “The truth of the matter is that I stopped doing it because the best political cartoons are really hard hitting, and I just, as an anchor, I just couldn’t do cartooning the way that it deserves to be done,” Tapper says. “I had to hold back. I had to pull punches. I had to run towards silly and inoffensive as opposed to hard hitting and brutal. And it just wasn’t as good. I wasn’t happy with it.” He’s had a lot of time to work on “The Butcher.” Tapper, who says he draws less frequently now, has been tough on himself. “After I finished the 250th page, I went back and redrew 100 pages because I’m like, those are awful. And I need to redraw them.” The recent practice has helped him regain some of his skill, he says, but “I’m still going back and tweaking.” One reason he embraced Top Shelf as his publisher is because he admired other graphic novels they have produced and he liked the fact that the editors there challenged him, with notes that could be “absolutely brutal.” Tapper embraced them. “I didn’t want it to be fast,” he says of the project. “I wanted it to be good.” He hopes the new graphic novel will have appeal. “It’s obviously a very serious topic, but it’s kind of a suspenseful book about how they track down this mass murderer who’d gotten away with it,” he says. “And then it gets into the politics of it, but in a very accessible way, about all the people that let this guy get away. I think anybody who’s interested in in a mystery, anybody who’s interested in World War II, anybody who’s interested in just a good yarn” will find something in the project. Tapper even worked with the daughter of Allan Ryan a former U.S. Department of Justice official who investigated how Barbie was able to avoid punishment for so long. He places Ryan in the graphic novel, where he serves as a sort of narrator. Tapper knows that some people may be surprised by his work in the medium, but believes the tale will win them over. “It’s not about 2026 politics at all,” he says. “It’s just a true story.” NFL on Sling TV 2026: Here’s How to Watch Minnesota Vikings vs. Chicago Bears Game Live Online Disney and NFL Team Up on Apparel Collection, Pairing Each of the League’s 32 Teams With Beloved Franchise Characters NFL Season 2026-2027 Livestream: Here’s Where to Watch Pro Football Games Online X Launches ‘NFL Gametime,’ a Football Feed Placed Alongside ‘For You’ and ‘Following’ Tony Romo Suggests He’d Like to Return to CBS’ NFL Coverage After No Contest Plea Netflix Taps ‘Friday Night Lights’ Director Peter Berg for NFL Gameday Openers, the First Narrated by Kyle Chandler Loading comments...

title: Russell Brand Told Fan To “Clean Up Mess” After Alleged Rape As Accuser Tells Court She “Carried Feeling Of Guilt & Shame” For Years
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Manager Spearheading Entertainment & New Media Biz At Three Six Zero Russell Brand Accuser Says She Reported Comedian To Channel 4 In 2009 After He Allegedly Lay His Head On Her Lap & Demanded Massage Russell Brand Accuser Alleges Witnesses Were Present When He “Grabbed My Face” & “Pushed His Body Against Mine” At Radio Station View All October 21, 2026 5:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday Getty Editor’s note: T his story contains details of alleged sexual offenses that readers may find distressing Russell Brand told one of his fans to “clean up the mess” after allegedly anally raping her at his home in north London, a court has been told. On a busy day at London’s Southwark Crown Court, the jury heard from three of Brand’s six accusers. The court was played a 2024 video recording of a police interview with one woman, whom we are calling Complainant 5 (C5) as she has a lifelong right to anonymity . During the two-hour-long interview, C5 was frequently in tears and distressed as she relived her alleged encounter with Brand. title: John C. Reilly, Penny Lane Board Short Doc ‘Stalin Boys’ as Executive Producers (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Stalin Boys' Courtesy of Pipsqueak Productions/Amplify Pictures Nonfiction filmmaker Penny Lane ( Confessions of a Good Samaritan ) and Academy Award-nominated actor John C. Reilly have boarded the short documentary film Stalin Boys as executive producers. Directed by Ora DeKornfeld and Bianca Giaever, the film follows Malachi, a middle school student in Marathon, Texas, who is obsessed with Joseph Stalin . Yes, THAT Joseph Stalin! When he hears about the Texas History Day competition, he writes a play about the late Soviet dictator and enlists his friends Cayden, Lyric and Jurem to play fearful civilians and loyal henchmen. Related Stories Business Audiovisual Women Leadership Program Unveils Participants, Sets Tallinn Partnership Business Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script “In a school of 11 students in a town of about 400, the boys grapple with a dark chapter of history and confront questions of power and legacy in their own lives,” a synopsis teases. The film debuted on The New York Times Op-Docs earlier this month and is eligible for the Academy Award for Documentary Short Film category. Veteran doc director Lane, whose subjects have ranged from Kenny G in Listening to Kenny G to Flaco the owl in Wild Inside , was drawn to what she described as the Little Miss Sunshine -esque blend of whimsy and heart. “I never imagined the words, ‘Screw National History Day!’ could make me laugh so hard and feel as much pain at the same time,” said Lane. “I’d also never thought to ask, ‘What was Stalin’s favorite color?’ but I’m glad to have met Malachi and discover he knows the answer.” Giaever lauded Lane as “a documentary icon,” adding: “Her work taught us that documentaries can be funny, playful, and absurd, while still tackling difficult topics.” Reilly will support the filmmakers’ campaign to bring Stalin Boys to classrooms and audiences nationwide. “I loved this short film,” the star said. “I loved it so much I lent my name to it as an executive producer. It reminded me of my own very imaginative and inspired childhood obsessions as a theater kid. I found the kids to be a wonderful inspiration to us all with their commitment to and enthusiasm for their vision. I also was deeply moved by the teachers who supported and guided them to realizing their visions. It takes caring people like these teachers to shepherd today’s young people if we want a better future for our world.” Concluded Reilly: “I hope everyone watches this film and remembers that big lives always start small and even tiny dusty towns in the middle of nowhere can produce people who can shape a brighter future for us all.” DeKornfeld said about Reilly: “John has spent his career playing people who are funny and heartbreaking in the same breath, which is exactly who these boys are. He immediately understood this film is about what’s possible when teachers encourage kids to follow their interests, as weird as they may be. We could not have asked for a better champion to help us get it in front of the audiences who need it most.” The filmmakers learned about the story while visiting their friend Crawford Hunt, who had been recruited to teach history at the school. They spent a week with the boys and their teachers during rehearsals for the state competition. Stalin Boys , which you can watch here, premiered at the Big Sky Documentary Film Festival and won the Audience Award and a Special Jury Award at the 2 026 SXSW Film & TV Festival. In July, the film also won the Academy Award-qualifying Documentary Grand Prize at Indy Shorts. It screens later this month at AFI Fest in Los Angeles. Stalin Boys was edited by Natalie Ancona, with an original score by Elori Saxl. The Pipsqueak Productions film was produced by Alejandra Vasquez and Amplify Pictures. For Op-Docs, Alexandra Garcia is the executive producer and Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo the producer. The short was supported by Southern Methodist University’s Narrative Now Initiative, Mountainfilm and The Economic Hardship Reporting Project. DeKornfeld directed the Emmy-nominated short USA v SCOTT , The Grandfather Puzzle and several episodes of the Netflix original series Explained . She is currently in production on a feature documentary about journalistic fixers in Mexico. Giaever is an independent filmmaker, radio journalist and the creator and host of the podcast Constellation Prize . Her upcoming documentary series Free Help premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival and will be available next year. THR

title: Audiovisual Women Leadership Program Unveils Participants, Sets Tallinn Partnership
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 5:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Audiovisual Women participants Courtesy of Erich Pommer Institut Germany’s Erich Pommer Institut (EPI) has unveiled the participants of its fifth edition of Audiovisual Women, its program designed for female professionals in mid- to senior-level management positions across the European audiovisual sector. The cohort includes 15 media professionals from 11 countries. “The program seeks to strengthen participants’ professional networks, unlock new business opportunities and support the sustainable growth of their careers and companies,” the EPI says. “Audiovisual Women helps female leaders navigate industry challenges, develop innovative business models and harness the opportunities of digital transformation.” The offering is open to female leaders working across the entire value chain of the industry. Participants go through a mix of in-person and online training sessions, one-on-one business coaching, exclusive networking events and a self-study phase. The goal is to strengthen leadership skills and explore key topics, including entrepreneurship, innovation, change management, communication and self-promotion. New this year is a partnership with the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event , the industry platform of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF). In mid-November, EPI will take the participants to Tallinn to give them the opportunity to expand their networks beyond their home markets and connect with professionals from across Europe. A distinctive feature of the program is its archery-based learning concept, developed by coach Annette Birkholz, which is designed to allow participants to connect, explore, and reflect on systemic patterns. By also involving participants’ hiring managers and encouraging more diverse, gender-balanced recruitment practices, Audiovisual Women further aims to foster “lasting structural change” across the industry. “With Audiovisual Women, we aim to strengthen female leadership and contribute to a more diverse, innovative and equitable audiovisual industry,” says Gabriela Seidel-Hollaender, project manager international training at EPI. “Investing in female leadership is essential to building a more resilient and forward-looking industry.” Audiovisual Women is funded by Creative Europe MEDIA. Partners of the program are FOCAL, Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), PÖFF – Black Nights Film Festival, Industry@ Tallinn & Baltic Event, EAVE – European Audiovisual Entrepreneurs, EWA – European Women’s Audiovisual Network, and Women in Film & Television International (WIFTI). title: Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth?
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 5:06am PT Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? 2 hours ago Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’ 17 hours ago Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Netflix Shares of Netflix hit a two-year low after the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings report revealed an ongoing softening in top-line growth and a miss on advertising revenue for the full year. The stock was down -7% in premarket trading Wednesday, to under $64/share, a decline of nearly 30% year-to-date to the lowest point since August 2024. Netflix’s Q4 revenue guidance was slightly below Wall Street expectations, and the company said ad sales for 2026 are now expected to be $2.7 billion, $300 million lighter than previously forecast, because of the slower-than-expected rollout of “some ad product capabilities.” Related Stories CMA's 'Celebration of Dolly Parton' Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire So how does Netflix recharge audience engagement (and therefore keep revenue pointed up) after a drop-off in viewing, particularly in the U.S. ? Popular on Variety To Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, the answer is better execution on its core model — that the company needs to crank up its buffet of buzzy, must-watch TV shows and movies. Last week he dismissed content chief Bela Bajaria, who’s being replaced by Peter Rice, as part of a larger overhaul of content leadership . On the Q3 earnings call, Sarandos praised Bajaria but said “I know that we could do better.” Ahead of its Q3 earnings, Netflix also laid off 1,000 workers , 6% of its headcount, which execs have framed as giving it the ability to invest more into growth areas. But some on Wall Street believe Netflix needs to do more than churn out TV and movie hits — that it needs a strategy to capture viewing of short-form video content, which is being soaked up by platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. “[W[e think the Street should remain skeptical of a long-term strategy that simply sees NFLX double down on its legacy core strength (premium TV, films, and increasingly, live events), while NFLX remains largely absent from the fastest areas video entertainment growth (e.g., mobile, short-form),” New Street Research analyst Dan Salmon wrote in an Oct. 20 research note. YouTube continues to make significant viewing share gains with an “all content types, all formats” approach on connected TV, Salmon wrote. While it doesn’t make sense for Netflix to adopt a straight user-generated content approach, he said, “we believe bold thinking is increasingly needed to address these long-term threats to NFLX mindshare with younger audiences.” Pivotal Research Group’s Jeff Wlodarczak similarly cited concerns for Netflix that short-form entertainment “is doing to streaming what streaming has done to traditional Pay TV,” as younger consumers spend an ever-increasing amount of time on social media platforms. Following Netflix’s Q3 earnings report, Wlodarczak reduced his subscriber forecasts and increased programming cost forecasts, leading to a $5 reduction in his year-end 2026 target price on the stock to $65. Meanwhile, Netflix once touted the addition of videogames as an extension of its core service as a promising growth driver — but games weren’t mentioned at all in its Q3 earnings, except that the company noted in its shareholder letter that it teamed up with Take-Two Interactive to unveil a sneak peek in August of highly anticipated title “Grand Theft Auto VI.” But all of that said, with over 325 million global subscribers, Netflix remains well positioned to keep its core streaming business humming along nicely, albeit at a somewhat less rapid clip, according to MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman. “We continue to believe Netflix has significant headspace to push monetization of its leading SVOD scale, which should lead to compounding profits for years to come,” Fishman wrote in a research note. MoffettNathanson forecasts Netflix earnings per share to reach $3.85 in 2027 (down from $4.00 previously), growing by 21% in 2028 to $4.65 (vs. $4.80 previously). The analyst reiterated a “buy” rating on Netflix stock but lowered his 12-month price target by $10 to $90/share. Also bullish on the long-term strategy was Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese, who wrote in a note that “the details suggest Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control.” She noted, “Churn and pricing held up, ad demand is intact, Netflix is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form.” “Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout,” Reese wrote. Because Netflix still has “significant potential” to expand ad revenue, Wedbush analysts reiterated their “outperform” rating on Netflix but lowered the price target on the stock from $90 to $80/share. title: Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 21, 2026 4:19am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos Andrew Leyden/Getty Images Netflix ‘s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings report is in, but what does it mean? In co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ telling, it’s all about execution. And how is Wall Street reacting to management commentary about the streaming giant’s outlook and largest layoffs in years, including the exit of film head Dan Lin and the replacement of chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice? Sarandos discussed content strategy, with co-CEO Greg Peters addressing a 2026 shortfall in advertising revenue. But the key quote from the call may have been Sarandos’ blunt note about staying the course. Related Stories Movies Camel Racing, a Sect and Workplace Democracy: Tallinn Fest Sets Docs Lineup, Special Screenings Movies Great Lakes Creative Producers Lab Unveils Cohort of 15 Film Producers From Seven African Countries “There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy,” he said. “We do need better execution in the U.S.” adding: “It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like. So we had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world.” In Wednesday pre-market trading, Netflix’s stock was down more than 6 percent at $64.35, signaling a new 52-week low. As of Tuesday’s market close, that low had been at $65.08. So, what can investors take away from the streamer’s updates? Below, The Hollywood Reporter has compiled analysts’ reactions to Netflix’s latest set of results and outlook. Analyst: Mark Mahaney, Evercore ISI Stock rating and price target: outperform, $90, down from $110 Takeaways: “Is A Better Script Coming?” was the key question that the analyst posed in the headline of his report. “For the third quarter in a row, Netflix shares traded off mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percentages in the aftermarket on soft earnings per share results. And this is now the fourth quarter in a row that Netflix guidance has come in lighter on at least one metric. Growth has clearly slowed at Netflix.” Mahaney reduced his financial estimates and pointed out slowed revenue growth, wondering: “What’s Going Wrong And Is There A Fix?” He then put forward some reasons: “We attribute this to some market maturity, consistent competition from large platforms like YouTube, Amazon, Disney, etc. … potentially a structural challenge from short-form content platforms (TikTok, YouTube again), and content mis-execution (i.e. no major global hits since KPop Demon Hunters ).” What to do? “We believe most of these challenges are addressable, and we view Netflix management as highly capable,” the analyst offered. “By bringing in a new chief content officer, Netflix is at least acknowledging and acting on the challenge. We also believe that Netflix, the global hit machine, will likely have a hit in 2027.” And Mahaney shared an upbeat conclusion. “This along with an improvement in content delivery and some key live events (Women’s World Cup) may well drive growth again in U.S. viewing hours, changing the engagement narrative. We also see live events and the expansion of the ad-supported plan to 15 new markets in 2027 as potentially accelerating sub ads growth,” he wrote. All in all, “we believe the Netflix long thesis is still intact. Or at least, we are more confident than the market is that it is intact.” Analyst: Brian Pitz, BMO Capital Markets Stock rating and price target: outperform, $125 Takeaways: “Advertising faces product delays, but [the] long-term vision [is] still intact,” was the analyst’s post-earnings takeaway, with results leading him to “fine-tune” his financial estimates. Despite ad momentum running behind expectations, the analyst continues to see advertising as a key growth opportunity for Netflix. “We remain positive on the long-term monetization opportunity and see the near-term advertising slowdown as buildout pain rather than a structural growth challenge,” he wrote. Content and subscriber momentum are a mixed bag. “Encouragingly, membership growth remains solid, supported by healthy subscriber retention across regions as churn improved year-over-year,” the analyst noted. “We were encouraged that Netflix’s industry-leading churn improved year-over-year globally and in the U.S., better than management expected. However, management acknowledged that U.S. content execution needs improvement, and the incoming chief content officer Peter Rice will focus on it.” Pitz also addressed the role sports could play in the content strategy. “While Netflix is unlikely to buy expensive season-long premium sports rights, it continues to lean into specific live inventory, adding its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game,” he said. “Live content accounts for only 1 percent of engagement hours despite representing 5 percent of content spend, but it remains an important lever for improving subscriber acquisition and retention and reducing churn.” Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim Stock rating and price target: buy, $78, down from $80 Takeaways: To explain his stock price target reduction, Morris cited “third-quarter results that met guidance but were paired with an outlook modestly short of expectations,” which led him to lower his 2027 revenue estimate to $56.8 billion from $57.1 billion, with his earnings per share forecast down by 9 cents to $3.80. With Netflix cutting its 2026 advertising revenue target to around $2.7 billion from $3.0 billion also made Morris pare back his 2027 ad estimate to $4.0 billion, which he said compares to a $5.2 billion consensus expectation. Of course, the recent content leadership changes and what it means for its programming strategy also featured in his report. “Co-CEO Ted Sarandos described the company’s strategy as ‘unchanged’ while acknowledging ‘we could do better,'” he wrote. “Peter Rice’s mandate as chief content officer is to find more home runs across formats and genres and strengthen talent relationships. Returning franchises including Emily in Paris , The Diplomat and Wednesday , and feature films including Narnia , provide a bridge to a lineup developed under Mr. Rice, and we consider a more impactful slate non-negotiable for renewed investor interest.” He also called content licensing “a silver lining” in content, citing a recent deal with Disney. Concluded Morris: “Netflix is a top platform for licensed product, and in our view more win-win partnerships with underexposed content at attractive terms would be incremental. Bundling with most other major streamers or launching a free service in the U.S. would not sustainably bolster top-line growth.” Analyst: Ralph Schackart, William Blair Stock rating and price target: outperform, no price target Takeaways: The engagement and content debates featured heavily in Schackart’s report. “The company acknowledged the need to accelerate view-hours growth, highlighting India as an example of successful execution, where view hours increased 24 year-over-year and view hours per member grew in the low- to mid-single digits,” he highlighted. The analyst also weighed in on Rice’s content chief appointment. “Management views the transition as an opportunity to improve content execution, particularly in the United States,” he wrote. “Management stressed that the change does not represent a shift in content strategy, but rather an opportunity to take the slate to the next level.” Schackart summarized his takeaways from the results and outlook this way: “Unfortunately, this quarter did not give the bears a reason to pull back on their growth concerns.” What does this mean for investors? “While it may take patience, we believe investors should benefit from accumulating shares on the pullback, recognizing that there is not a near-term catalyst. We believe the company will solve its near-term content concern at some point in 2027.” Analyst: Laurent Yoon, Bernstein Stock rating and price target: outperform, $80, down from $95 Takeaways: Patience was a recurring theme in Yoon’s report, which is entitled “When Success Starts Looking Mature.” “New content boss, new content strategy?” it asked. “Perhaps, but not anytime soon,” it offered. “Despite new leadership with deep experience across TV, film, and streaming, the messaging remains firmly centered on traditional content, live events, and licensing. Any meaningful strategic shift – if there’s one – could take years, not quarters, to show up in the slate or the numbers.” That may also keep weighing on investor sentiment. “Investors will increasingly focus on the durability of ‘double-digit’ growth and the pace of margin expansion as content investment comes back into focus,” the analyst explained. “The risk is not the near-term fundamentals, but perception. A strategy that continues to lean on traditional content, traditional formats, and traditional engagement risks reminding both consumers and investors of the ‘L’ word – legacy. That alone may be enough to keep the stock range-bound near term, even if the underlying business continues to execute well.” Advertising may not be broken, but also made for a disappointment. “Management discussed slower ad product rollouts rather than demand, suggesting a delay rather than disruption, but it still represents a missed opportunity,” the analyst concluded. All in all, he reduced its forecasts for Netflix, which also pushed down the stock price target. “Changes in earnings per share estimates are due to slower-than-expected advertising revenue growth, domestic subscriber growth and margin expansion slightly offset by accelerated buybacks,” Yoon noted. “We also reduced our valuation multiple to 20 times (from 25 times) to reflect slower growth and ongoing negative investor sentiment without a near-term positive catalyst.” Analyst: Rob Fishman, MoffettNathanson Stock rating and price target: buy, $90, down from $100 Takeaways: MoffettNathanson was among the firms cutting their financial forecasts and Netflix stock price target, in this case by $10, following the latest results and management commentary. Fishman wondered about the outlook for revenue growth, especially given the ad revenue updates, and the outlook for content spending following the recent executive changes. “If revenue is slowing, does Netflix need to reaccelerate content spend?” the analyst asked. And he shared that underlying his forecast is 8 percent content spending growth as “management is clearly focused on reining in expenses to invest in high-impact areas, as evidenced by the recent headcount reductions.” His conclusion is that Netflix can continue to improve the monetization of its reach and scale to grow profits in the future. Wrote Fishman: “After the sell-off, we believe Netflix’s downside is limited, and the stock presents an attractive entry point to capture upside in leveraging the company’s global scale to drive incremental growth above the strength of its core business model.” THR

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Commish Domingo Corral Touts HBO Max TV Deal: “I’ve Found a Home”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 21, 2026 4:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'La Bola Negra' Carla Oset/Netflix Former Moviestar Plus+ fiction and entertainment head Domingo Corral intends to continue being Domingo Corral after striking an overall first-look TV deal with HBO Max. “I found a home,” Corral the former director of original content at Movistar Plus+ until he was fired in 2025 told The Hollywood Reporter on Wednesday while attending the MIA Market in Rome. “It’s like a new home, because I feel fortunate to have found a place where they want to do the same things that I want to do, and that’s amazing,” he added. While at the Spanish pay-TV and streaming giant, Corral gave a green light to Cannes breakout films like Oliver Laxe’s Oscar-nominated drama Sirât , Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s La Bola Negra, a epic about gay men in war-torn Spain and the Spanish entry for best international feature film at the Oscars, the Javier Bardem drama The Beloved, from director Rodrigo Sorogoyen, and director Alauda Ruiz de Azua’s Sundays. La Bola Negra was acquired by Netflix out of the Cannes Film Festival for an awards season push. The platform’s long release in theaters started on Oct. 16, ahead of streaming on Dec. 2. With success like that, Corral’s sudden exit from Movistar Plus+ led 144 members of the Spanish creative community, including Bardem, Penélope Cruz and Pedro Almodóvar, to sign an open letter in support of the producer, warning of the damage his exit could have on the Spanish industry. Now with his own indie production banner backed by the Warner Bros. Discovery streamer newly-acquired by Paramount Skydance, Corral said of his exclusive TV series collaboration: ‘I’m very happy I can work with HBO, because it’s very important to work with a commissioner that wants to make the same type of shows that I want to make, and that we share the same vision and the same passion for quality TV.” The first TV series from that overall deal is the 1980s-set El Nani, about a petty criminal from the Spanish slums wrongly arrested amid Spain’s transition from fascism to democracy, and to be written and directed by Alberto Rodríguez and Rafael Cobos ( The Anatomy of a Moment ). Expect few series from a “focused” producer, Corral insisted, and TV shows that bring on board the best Spanish creative talent he often worked with while at MovieStar Plus+. At the same time, now for the first time with a global streamer in HBO Max, Corral understands he will need to make series specific to Spain’s political and cultural reality that also potentially resonate worldwide. “I have an amazing opportunity to work for a streamer that is global and that a show I’m making for Spain can be seen all over the world,” he argued. Of course, for that vision to be realized, HBO Max under Paramount Skydance will need to continue being HBO. Corral has no crystal ball, but the early omens are promising after Casey Bloys signed a new multiyear deal to oversee HBO Max and Paramount+ in a new role at Skydance. “That’s really, really positive… It would have been bad news for HBO if that hadn’t happened. Fortunately it has happened. So I’m optimistic,” Corral told THR . THR

title: BBC Scraps TikTok Generation TV News Bulletin ‘The Catch Up’

The BBC has canned The Catch Up as part of the planned closure of BBC Three , the youth network that will be switched off for a second time in spring 2027. BBC Three ‘s brand will be retained on iPlayer. The Catch Up was launched in 2022 and was pitched as an attempt to “bring back” 16- to 24-year-old viewers to traditional news bulletins. Its debut coincided with BBC Three being restored to linear TV, a decision that was reversed on Tuesday. Related Stories Acquisitions The BBC & MHz Choice Board Sweden's Latest 'Wallander' Series News BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures The two- to four-minute news bulletin was designed to provide young viewers with a roundup of the day’s headlines in an accessible format, complete with graphics and a conversational tone. Watch on Deadline Tuesday’s bulletin was hosted by BBC journalist Ben Henley-Washford and featured a report on BBC Three’s demise as a linear television network. “The BBC has announced it is closing BBC Three,” Henley-Washford said. “Not just yet, though. They said the TV channel, along with BBC Scotland’s channel, will close in the spring as the corporation continues to make £500 million pounds worth of savings by 2028.” He did not mention that The Catch Up would be discontinued. When The Catch Up launched, then editor Amanda Goodman told Press Gazette : “We want to create relatable news for young people that doesn’t necessarily sound like the BBC, or the BBC they think exists at present.” BBC News was not on TikTok in 2022, but this has changed. The BBC News account now has 16.5 million followers and more than 1 billion likes. A BBC News spokesperson said: “The BBC is the UK’s leading news publisher for 16-34 year olds in the UK – reaching around half of 16–34-year-olds each week across its BBC News platforms, including youth-focused offerings such as Newsbeat , as well as Newsround for a younger audience. “Further to this, there are significant and growing numbers of young people accessing BBC News across our social channels – including TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. title: Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:05am PT Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says 3 hours ago ‘Deadstream’ Directors Joseph and Vanessa Winter to Helm Horror Movie ‘Future Me’ as Longevity Pictures, Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios Ink Multi-Picture Deal (EXCLUSIVE) 22 hours ago Raj Singh and Italy’s RP1 Holding Launch €100 Million Film Fund to Boost Country’s Struggling Indie Ecosystem 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "The Monster of Florence" (Courtesy of Emanuela Scarpa/Netflix) Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming. That is the main takeaway from a report issued on Wed. by Italian TV producers’ association APA during Rome’s MIA market, which is dedicated to international TV series, animation, feature films and documentaries. Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates which remained firmly in place. Popular on Variety “This situation hinders producers’ ability to plan, increases financial burdens, and shrinks profit margins,” the report pointed out. “It negatively impacts all companies — especially smaller ones — by straining liquidity and limiting their capacity for future investment,” is added. Hopefully, there is some relief in sight with the new tax credit now in place. The so-called application “window” to apply has been reopened. The report underlined that unscripted content remains the backbone of Italian broadcasting programming, with an output of over 17,000 hours of original, first-run content, being churned out by Italian producers last year. Independent production accounts for 59% of these titles. Unscripted offerings from streaming platforms in Italy have also expanded, with a 51% increase in the number of titles and a 30% rise in total hours. Within Italy’s unscripted sphere, the factual genre has seen the most significant growth, up 36% in terms of number of hours, with the number of domestic factual titles adapted from international formats doubling. Game shows are also gaining ground on linear networks, both in early evening and prime time slots. As for scripted originals, the number of titles in 2025 grew 9% to a total 101 shows produced for the current season. But this growth is driven primarily by 74 smaller domestic series for linear networks, that don’t tend to travel, while the number of Italian originals served up by streamers last year stands the same as 2024 with 27 titles, most of which are, similarly, “local for local” product. The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighbourhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.” The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “ The Monster of Florence ,” pictured above, directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025. Meanwhile, as in the rest of the world, the market share for linear television (both free-to-air and pay-TV) is steadily shrinking in Italy while global platforms continue to grow. The streaming segment, which accounted for 21% of the market in 2020, has now reached 43% in the Italian market and “is set to surpass linear television in value in the short-to-medium term,” the report said. Also in line with global TV trends, microdramas are starting to gain traction in Italy with ReelShort, DramaBox, NetShort, and DramaWave already among the country’s top fifteen entertainment apps in terms of user spend, the report said. And the first original Italian microdrama production has been released, titled “Tutto in una notte,” produced by Fascino PGT, with its 54 episodes distributed on Italian platform WittyTV and on social media.
