title: ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 21, 2026 4:04am PT ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘When I Existed,’ a Cannes Market Standout, Swooped On for World Sales by M-Appeal and Now Bound for Tallinn Black Nights (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source When I Existed (Courtesy of M-Appeal) Berlin-based M-Appeal has boarded “ When I Existed ,” a buzzy, feel-good second-chance drama comedy and Kafkian social satire which proved a standout at the Cannes Market’s Ventana Sur Goes to Cannes showcase, marking an auspicious debut for Uruguay’s Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov. A select but discerning sales agent of Latin American movies, M-Appeal has picked up international sales on “When I Existed” (“Cuando yo existía”) just weeks before the feature’s world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . Related Stories Discovery+, Now Owned by Skydance, Hikes Prices Effective Immediately The feature debut of writer-directors by Damiani and Martin Avdolov, “When I Existed” unfolds its humane modern parable when Silvio Bertolini retires after spending 40 years building Uruguay’s foremost gates construction company. Popular on Variety Attempting to draw his pension, and with his credit cards frozen, he discovers that the National Pension and Retirement Fund, also his bank, register him as deceased. Sent from pillar to post – to the bank’s Accounts, Payments and Claims treading dark puddled basement corridors and joining seemingly interminable lines. He meanwhile reconnects with old friends from his sculling boat club of youth, and re-awakes – but is it too late? – to what it really means to be alive: Spending time with his wife who hopes retirement will open a new chapter in their life together. Driving “When I Existed” is a notably modulated performance from César Troncoso, star of “The Pope’s Toilet” and “The Eternaut,” as Silvio, ranging from smiling containment of a reasonable man to outraged anger, paralysis from anxiety, wistful regret and lovelorn solitude. Silvia Kutica (“Avellaneda’s Moon,” “Argentina, Land of Love and Revenge”) plays Silvio’s now increasingly estranged wife of 40 years. “When I Existed” is lead produced by Federico Cetta for Uruguay’s El Cielo Cine who describes as “a story of reinvention built around the things that truly matter.” Structured as near any film of ambition these days an as international co-production, “When I Existed” is co-produced by David Matamoros at Barcelona’s Doce Entertainment and Andrés Rosenblatt at Montevideo’s Metropolis Films as co-producers. Matías Burgos at Moon Ideas, also based out of Montevideo, serves as associate producer. “This story speaks to us in a world where we have the constant feeling that time is slipping away between obligations we don’t always choose,” said Avdolov. “What do we do with the time we have? Today we need small acts of resistance against a logic that tends to make everything increasingly automatic and artificial. For me, making this film has something of that.” “What won us over about ‘When I Existed’ was its rare mix of humor and humanity,” said M-Appeal founder Maren Kroymann. She added: “Silvio is a charming man who struggles to accept retirement, while his wife has been waiting for this moment, hoping they can finally enjoy life together. Their story is both touching and deeply relatable, reminding us how easily we can get caught up in our habits and lose sight of what matters most. It’s a film that makes you laugh, moves you, and reminds us that it’s never too late to reconnect with the people we love.” ‘When I Existed,’ Broken Down by Damiani and Avdolov “When I Existed” is shot with unusual elegance but sense of humor by Manuel Branaa, a camera operator on J.A. Bayona’s Netflix smash-hit “Society of the Snow.” This is caught in the the lateral tracking shot with which it opens, crossing a dark granite stone tomb taking in the red and yellows of flowers left on it. Asethetically, it’s a highly pleasing composition, but the flowers are wilting. Drawing a counterpoint between the open expanses of marshlands, where Silvio catches up with his boat club best friends of youth, the charcoal grey and black corridors and barred doors and windows of the National Pension and Retirement Fund’s labyrinthine office conveys a sense of claustrophobia – that of a man caught not only in a bureaucratic system but his own self-absorption. “When I Existed” delves into “the nature of the system, the ego, bureaucracy, technological trends, the dangers of alienation, and the erosion of humanity,” said Damiani and Avdolov. “We poured our souls into even the smallest details – things that might go unnoticed by others, but which, to us, made the work feel complete and purposeful,” they added. Damiani has worked for years in advertising, as a copywriter and designer, wining Uruguay’s fist Golden Lion, then in VFX rising to Creative Director at top Uruguayan VFX house Aparato. Avdolov has transitioned to filmmaking from a career as a novelist (“Violeta Corazón,” “Camba”), short-story writer and author of the non-fiction “El Corazón Creativo” (“The Creative Heart”). “When I Existed” is born from the deepest fear any human being can have: how are we supposed to live? No one teaches you that,” Damiani told Variety . It is also semi-autobiographical. “Working on ‘When I Existed’ made us realize how much of ourselves we poured into the film’s protagonist,” they added. “For many years, we had channeled our energy and creativity into other people’s projects. Following the pandemic – and having passed the age of 40– we decided to commit ourselves to our own meaningful projects. We see this film as a reminder that we are not here to live someone else’s life; Damiani’s 2016 short, “M.A.M.O.N. (Monitor Against Mexicans Over Nationwide),” went viral, hitting over 13 million views on YouTube. El Cielo Cine Of features, “El Cielo Cine” has produced with Argentina 2025’s well-received adopted son drama “Emi,” directed by Ezequiel Erríquez, and Santiago Giralt’s 2023 “Norma,” a later-life self-discovery tale starring and co-written by Mercedes Morán (“Neruda,” “My Sad Dead”) which scored a best comedy Platino Award nomination. title: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Manager Spearheading Entertainment & New Media Biz At Three Six Zero

title: How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan Disney Appoints Carol Choi As Asia Pacific President Following Luke Kang’s Retirement View All October 21, 2026 3:27am Add us as a Google Preferred Source TIFFCOM 2025 TIFFCOM At this year’s Marché du Film at the Cannes film festival, it would be no exaggeration to say that Japanese content and creators were everywhere you turned. Designated ‘Country of Honour’ at the market, Japan was involved in a slew of panels, workshops and labs; played a prominent role in Cannes flagship programs, including Cannes Animation, Co-Production Day, and Producers Network; and also launched the Japan IP Market, a three-day initiative co-hosted by the Marché and Japan’s leading contents market TIFFCOM . The Marché decided to shine a spotlight on Japan in recognition of the strength of its content and intellectual property (IP), as well as recent efforts – by the Japanese government, local studios, and independent filmmakers and producers – to engage with the rest of the world. As Deadline noted at TIFFCOM two years ago, Japan was once reliant on its huge domestic market, but is now actively seeking co-production, collaboration and exports, focusing its efforts on North and South America, Europe, and the rest of Asia. Related Stories Executives Amazon MGM Studios Elevates Julie Rapaport & Alana Mayo In Film Division Reorg News 'Lizard Music' Starring Dwayne Johnson And Directed By Benny Safdie To Tune Up Christmas Day 2027 Via Amazon MGM All these efforts are being supported by the Japanese government, which last year launched the ‘Content Industry Growth Investment Support Program’, branded as IP360, which aims to expand overseas sales of Japanese content (across film, anime, games and music) to $126BN (JPY20 trillion) by 2033. Watch on Deadline “Historically, sectors including Japanese anime and live-action content have been optimized for the domestic market, lacking an industrial structure designed to expand into global markets,” explains TIFFCOM CEO Yasushi Shiina. “At Cannes this year, as the Country of Honour, the public and private sectors joined forces to showcase Japan’s key strengths, including anime and manga. In doing so, we built networks with international producers, distributors, and other industry professionals, driving strong momentum toward transforming the sector into an IP-driven industry that generates global revenue. “Following this, TIFFCOM will leverage the home-ground advantage of being hosted in Japan to promote Japanese IP alongside a diverse array of participants. For international attendees as well, we aim to make TIFFCOM a platform where they can connect directly with Japanese partners and unlock new business opportunities.” Yasushi Shiina [L] & Kaori Ikeda [R] A key program within TIFFCOM is the Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake (TIPM), an initiative that the Cannes IP event was also based on, which brings together publishers and production companies holding rights to Japanese manga, audiovisual works, novels and games. This year, the number of participating IP holders has expanded from six to ten companies, including content giants such as Amuse Creative Studio, Kadokawa, Nippon Animation, Shochiku and Toei . TIPM organizes a series of one-on-one meetings between the rights holders and international producers, mostly from North America, Europe and the rest of Asia. In addition, eight of these companies will hold an open pitch event, with audiovisual support from Imagica Group, to present their flagship IP. “We co-organized the Japan IP Market in Cannes – the Cannes edition of TIPM – with the Marché du Film, and the event generated an exceptionally strong response,” explains TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda. “Thanks to this success, the Tokyo edition is seeing an increasing number of leading producers attending from Europe and Hollywood. We’re excited to offer everyone in Tokyo this premier opportunity to connect with high-quality Japanese IP.” Another key TIFFCOM track is the Tokyo Gap Financing Market (TGFM), which presents projects with Asian elements and at least 60% of their funding in place, that are seeking to complete their budgets through co-production, sales, distribution and other forms of investment. This year, the event has selected 24 projects including Vincci Cheuk’s Hong Kong-Japan co-production 38.83 ; Boo Junfeng’s multi-territory co-production Trinity ; François-Marc Baillet’s animated feature Back To Tomioka ; five projects selected through a partnership with Canada’s Frontières genre market, and three in partnership with Italy’s Cinecitta ( see here for the full list of selected projects ). In addition, TGFM talk sessions will introduce Japan’s various support schemes – including grants for international co-productions from Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunka-cho) – alongside funding from Canada and Brazil. Japanese producers have been co-producing with their East Asian neighbors in Taiwan and South Korea for quite some time but have recently been venturing further afield into Southeast Asia and Europe. “Two factors are driving this,” says Ikeda. “First, production volume is increasing across Asia as a whole, including Southeast Asia, and production capabilities are also rising. “Second, opportunities to build networks with one another at film festivals and markets across Asia are expanding. Platforms such as TGFM are facilitating mutual introductions, leading to an increasing number of co-production projects with Southeast Asia. Japan also recently joined the new Asian Producers Alliance with the Agency for Cultural Affairs as the representative member.” In Europe, co-productions between Japan and France have been the most common, but Ikeda observes that projects with Italy have also increased following the signing of an official Japan-Italy co-production treaty in 2024. Recent co-productions involving Japan include Sleep No More , from Indonesian filmmaker Edwin, which premiered at this year’s Berlinale; Ria , from the Philippines’ Arvin Belarmino, which won the Heart of Eurasia Award at Busan film festival, and Boo’s upcoming Trinity , which has around ten co-producers across Europe and Asia. Trinity , Ria and Janus Victoria’s Japan-Philippines co-production Diamonds In The Sand were all selected for various editions of TGFM. ‘Ria’ Meanwhile, TIFFCOM’s conference program will present around 20 sessions organized along thematic lines: intellectual property (IP), artificial intelligence (AI), Japanese TV, Asian Series & Films, market trends and co-production. Key sessions include an ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’, with speakers from Credeus ( Kokuho ), Amazon MGM Studios and Netflix’s One Piece ; an AI-themed keynote with AGBO ’s Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes; and the annual session by the Association of Japanese Animations, presenting data on the anime industry. Leading Japanese broadcasters Nippon TV and TBS will host sessions on their international activities; an Anime Co-Production Conference will feature speakers including Ervin Han ( The Violinist ), and a “Beyond Country of Honour” session has speakers from Toho and K2 Pictures, along with TIFFCOM’s Shiina and Cannes Marché Head of Industry Programs Alexandra Zakharchenko. Last year’s TIFFCOM had more than 4,600 attendees from 46 countries and regions, an increase of 13% from the previous year, while international participation rose by 10%. As of two weeks before this year’s edition, Ikeda says that visitor registrations – mostly buyers and producers – were up about 10% on the same point last year. “East Asia continues to drive strong participation, led by Taiwan and South Korea, as well as a dedicated pavilion from Thailand,” Ikeda says. “Some companies from China, including streaming platforms, will also take part. And in a notable new trend, we are also seeing increasing participation from companies offering AI and data analytics solutions.” TIFFCOM is taking place October 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho district, which is just a few train stops away from Tokyo International Film Festival’s main venues in Hibiya-Ginza. The festival is running from October 26 to November 4. title: Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz How TIFFCOM Is Building On Cannes Recognition To Strengthen Global Networks, Co-Production & Japanese IP Tokyo Film Festival Chiefs Talk Balancing Blockbusters & Arthouse; Launching International Films In Japan Disney Appoints Carol Choi As Asia Pacific President Following Luke Kang’s Retirement View All October 21, 2026 3:24am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Godzilla Minus Zero Toho It’s an exciting time for Japanese cinema, with franchise hits from Demon Slayer to Godzilla stomping around the world, and Japanese arthouse titles taking the spotlight at major film festivals including Venice, Toronto and Cannes. This year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, taking place in the Hibiya-Ginza district of the city from October 26 to November 4, aims to take full advantage of the momentum and help expand the international profile of Japanese films. Under incoming Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu, and Programming Director Shozo Ichiyama, the festival is also positioning itself as a launchpad for international films in Japan. Related Stories Commentary We Can See Oscar Possibilities For A24's Hit Documentary 'You Can See Everything' - And That Includes An Acting Category News 'La Bola Negra' Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became "The Journey Of Our Lives" Hisamatsu, who previously held senior posts at Warner Bros Japan and local studio Shochiku, headed the festival from 2017-2021 and returned earlier this year when Hiroyasu Ando stepped down after seven years at the helm. While Ichiyama has been strengthening the festival’s competitions, Gala and World Focus line-ups, Hisamatsu says he wants to bolster the glamour quotient at the festival, especially as it gears up for its 40th edition next year. Watch on Deadline “We want to combine art and entertainment and make the festival as multifaceted as possible,” says Hisamatsu, sitting down with Deadline at the festival’s office in the historic Togeki Building in Ginza. “This should be a festival for cinephiles, for general film fans, and also for people who maybe only visit a cinema once or twice in a year. Everyone should be able to find something they want to see.” While describing this year’s pre-anniversary edition as a time for evaluation, he envisages a line-up that includes Japanese films, Hollywood and other international titles, awards contenders, and every genre and format from live action and animation to documentary and short films. The U.S. studios have not been promoting heavily at Asian film festivals in recent years, but Hisamatsu hopes to lure them back: “Japan is still a big market – last year our box office hit a record and surpassed pre-pandemic revenues. Now is a good time to reboot the popularity of Hollywood films in Japan.” Hisamatsu is also engaging with international organisations, including the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences ( AMPAS ), which is bringing a delegation of executives, including Academy CEO Bill Kramer, to participate in a busy schedule of panels and networking events at the festival. Several awards season contenders, including Wild Horse Nine , La Bola Negra , animated feature Wildwood , and Christian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord , are screening across the festival’s Gala, World Focus and Special Screenings sections. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures However, the festival toppers stress that this doesn’t mean any attention will be taken away from Japanese titles. “One of our major goals is to introduce Japanese films to international markets,” says Hisamatsu. The festival will open with a Japanese film – Zeze Takahisa’s Sukiyaki , about the historic song that topped the Billboard charts and remains one of the world’s best-selling tunes – while Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus Zero , the highly-anticipated sequel to Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One , will play as the Centerpiece Film. Korean filmmaker Yang Sang-ho’s zombie thriller Colony will close the festival. Three Japanese films have been selected for the festival’s main Competition section: The Canary’s Lullaby , directed by Akira Ikeda; Yukiko Mishima’s Two Cigarettes, Three Nights ; and Akira Yamamoto’s The Intertwining . Ichiyama, the festival’s Programming Director, explains that The Canary’s Lullaby is a Japan-Taiwan co-production, partly filmed on Taiwan’s Kinmen Island, and The Intertwining is based on a Japanese novel but has Korean elements, demonstrating the more international outlook of Japan’s new generation of directors. With major festivals including Cannes, Venice and Toronto, all of which take place before Tokyo, hoovering up Japanese titles over the past few years, Ichiyama says his focus has been on discoveries, as the festival requires world premieres for the Japanese films in competition. “These three filmmakers are not so well known internationally, but they’re all extremely promising, and have the potential to go to European film festivals in the future,” he says. Takeo Hisamatsu [L] & Shozo Ichiyama [R] Other world premieres in the Competition line-up include Indonesian filmmaker Garin Nugroho’s Red Before Dawn , set in a newly independent Indonesia in the 1940s, which Ichiyama describes as “a big-budget epic drama”; Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski’s social satire Sister Brother Manhole Cover ; and two Chinese-language titles Fuxi: Four Tales Of Feasting , from Qiu Jiongjiong, and Wang Jianyong’s The Night That Binds Us . Also in the line-up of 15 competition titles is Rubaiyat Hussain’s The Difficult Bride , which world premiered in the Horizons section of this year’s Venice film festival and marks the first ever Bangladeshi film selected for Tokyo main competition. “We saw it in Venice and sent the the invitation very quickly,” says Ichiyama. “We usually see two or three interesting films from Bangladesh in one year, and this one is outstanding.” Rounding out the competition are Heysel 85 , from Romanian filmmaker Teodora Ana Mihai, joining Tokyo Competition for the third time following Traffic and La Civil ; Until The Day Ends , from Serbian filmmaker Jelena Maksimović; Double Freedom , from Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso; Even If Hell Came , from Italy’s Samuele Rossi; Portuguese filmmaker Sérgio Graciano’s Memories Of Prison ; Singaporean animation Magic Atlas from Sun Xun, and Trees Are Watching from Iranian-Kurdish filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi. ‘Heysel 85’ Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer is heading the main competition jury, which also includes Tokyo and New York-based producer Alex Lo, Korean producer Oh Jungwan, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe. An Australia Spotlight will screen De Heer’s 2022 The Survival Of Kindness ; Natalie Erika James’ body horror Saccharine , and Vee Shi’s hybrid documentary Time And Tide . Other talent attending the festival include Cate Blanchett , in town to celebrate the Japan premieres of five short films supported by the Displacement Film Fund (and who is also a producer on Alpha Gang , recently added to Special Screenings); as well as Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof and Japanese filmmaker Mipo O, both recipients of this year’s Kurosawa Akira Award. Filmmakers including Ilya Khrzhanovsky ( DAU ), Teodora Ana Mihai ( Heysel 85 ), Zeze Takahisa ( Sukiyaki ), Shahrbanoo Sadat ( No Good Men ) and Yukiko Sode ( All The Lovers In The Night ) will deliver talk sessions and masterclasses. Tokyo has two other competition sections – Asian Future, focused on emerging Asian directors, and Nippon Cinema Now, which aims to present an overview of the current state of contemporary Japanese film. Nippon Cinema Now will screen eight titles, from both new and established directors, and has introduced two new awards for Best Film and a Special Jury Prize. Asian Future, programmed by Kenji Ishizaka, will screen 10 world premieres from Japan, Korea, Philippines, India, Turkey, Kazakhstan, Indonesia and Iran. This year also sees the return of the festival’s non-competitive section dedicated to Southeast Asian cinema, Crosscut Asia, held in partnership with the Japan Foundation, which stopped running during the pandemic period. Now titled Crosscut Asia+, the section will screen three recent festival hits, Four Seasons In Java , Filipiñana and Becoming Human , along with a selection of retrospective titles. ‘ Iron Boy ‘ Other major sections include Animation, which will screen Cannes Un Certain Regard special jury prize winner Iron Boy , among other titles; Women’s Empowerment, including recent festival breakouts Lovers In The Blue Night , from India’s Anupama Roy, and A Girl Unknown , from China’s Zou Jing; Japanese Classics, including a Kenji Mizoguchi retrospective; and the Youth and Asian Students Film Conference sections. Taking place towards the end of the year, Tokyo Film Festival has always been in a good position to present a “best of fests” round-up for local audiences, and this year aims to double down on efforts to connect international films with Japanese buyers, both directly at the festival and through the TIFFCOM contents market taking place a few metro stops away. “Especially in World Focus, we’re showing many films that played in Berlin, Venice and Cannes, several of which have still not found a Japanese distributor,” Ichiyama says. “Japan has many strong, independent buyers, but with the current weakness of the Japanese yen, they’ve not been so eager to travel to Venice and Toronto or acquire new films. We can present those titles here in theatres with local audiences and Japanese subtitles.” With many screenings already sold out, filmmakers and industry can expect packed houses and attentive audiences for these films. As Hisamatsu observes, Japan continues to be one of the world’s top theatrical markets, and while anime and Godzilla may be pulling the biggest crowds, Tokyo Film Festival is one time of year at least when movies of all genres, languages and budget levels will be reaching audiences on a big screen. The festival kicks off on Monday, October 26, with an opening ceremony and screening of Sukiyaki, and runs until Wednesday, November 4, while TIFFCOM is taking place October 28-30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho. title: “Horror Is Now Cool” as the Hunt for the Next ‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ Is on: Rome’s MIA
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 21, 2026 3:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kane Parsons and Curry Barker Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/Getty Images; Amanda Edwards/Getty Images Horror industry leaders came to Rome to praise Curry Barker and Kane Parsons — the YouTubers-turned-directors behind the breakout Obsession and Backrooms horror movies. “The stigma of horror of the past, that it was niche, is past. Horror is now cool, and that’s great,” Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of Wonder Pictures, which released Backrooms in Italy, told a panel on the genre at the MIA Market in Rome. Peter Kuplowsky, programmer of the Toronto Film Festival’s thrills and spills Midnight Madness showcase, said the Hollywood box office rebound has helped underpin the resurgence in horror films. Related Stories Movies Seth Rogen Watched Curry Barker's Next Movie, Says It's "Even Better" Than 'Obsession' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast 'Obsession' Star Inde Navarrette on Sudden Fame, Cut Scenes, Relationship Takeaways, a Possible Sequel and Going Rogue for Marvel “The U.S. theatricals have bounded back, and there’s been an excitement to watch a movie with a movie again,” he insisted. So the hunt for Gen Z-tinged horror talent will continue. Including in Italy. Romeo after Backrooms wants more box office success: “We started to look for the next Kane Parsons and Oz Perkins. But we also want to find the Italian Kane Parsons. There’s some screenwriters and directors who want to be the next Kane Parsons. But they want to work in English. So we want to understand how to build an Italian background.” At the same time, the Italian Kane Parsons may be a woman. “A young female director will be my dream,” Romeo added. The horror leaders argued non-traditional horror directors like Parsons and Barker had come out of YouTube to offer fresh, new voices and innovation to the fright-night medium for Gen Z movie-goers. Rachael Labes, manager, acquisitions & productions for IFC’s Shudder, said horror films embracing comedy had also opened up new audiences. “There were 10 years where we were getting harsh movies. Now I can go to see a horror film that scares me, but also offers a fun time,” Labes argued. At the multiplex, Barker’s Obsession grossed over $400 million globally on a $750,000 budget and became Focus Features’ highest-grossing release ever. Meanwhile, Parsons’ Backrooms crossed $350 million in box office globally and is A24’s highest-grossing film in a number of countries. Roberto De Feo, an Italian director and screenwriter, says the breakout success of Obsession and Backrooms has allowed Paolo Strippoli’s campy, fun Italian horror thriller The Spiral , which bowed in Venice and is now potentially up for an Oscar. “It’s important to talk about the fact that the audience were used for 30 years to watch movies form the U.S., which was far from the Italian aesthetic. Now they want to see movies that are connected with Italy,” De Feo said. Jonny Bunning, digital marketing manager for UK-based Signature Entertainment, said horror films from new international filmmakers and exotic countries are having success connecting with audiences. “The genre community is interested to hear from a different community to see the different countries’ interpretation of horror and seeing visuals that you’re not familiar with, and that cuts through and piques that interest,” he told the panel. title: Jane Tranter Calls For “Stories That Change The Lack Of Empathy In Our World” & Reveals How James Gandolfini Influenced Bad Wolf
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Jane Tranter Calls For “Stories That Change The Lack Of Empathy In Our World” & Reveals How James Gandolfini Influenced Bad Wolf Prime Video Adds Sony LIV To Indian Offer Ex-Disney, NBCU & Bloomberg TV Execs Among New Advisory Board At Storyboarding Platform Pzaz View All October 21, 2026 3:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jane Tranter on stage at the MIA Market in Rome MIA The Other Bennet Sister producer Jane Tranter has launched an impassioned plea for TV makers to search out stories that “that will make our world a more empathetic place.” In a keynote talk at MIA Market this week, the Bad Wolf Production CEO and co-founder used the example of a “farmer in his 70s” who had identified with Mary, the outcast protagonist of BBC period drama The Other Bennet Sister played by the 30-year-old Ella Bruccoleri. “Being able to make a drama in 2026 that features a woman who some people in society doesn’t think should be an acceptable face of a woman,” said Tranter. Related Stories News 'Industry' Star Myha'la Claims "Unconscious Racial Bias" Is Baked Into 'The Traitors' News International Insider: 'Doctor Who' Regeneration Underway; MIPCOM Preview; Busan Takeaways “She doesn’t look like what people want her to look like, she doesn’t sound like what people want her to sound like and she doesn’t behave like society wants a woman to behave like and yet she is her own woman. Watch on Deadline “In 2026, stories about people being accepted for who they choose to be are the kind of stories I will keep making until someone carries me out in a wooden box. I really urge you to look for those stories. We have to tell stories that change the lack of empathy in our world. Look into yourselves and go and tell your own stories that will make our world a more empathetic place.” The Other Bennet Sister is an adaptation of former BBC executive Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name. The BBC series, which plays on BritBox in the U.S., tells the story of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice from the viewpoint of Mary, the overlooked sister from the Bennet family, before telling the tale of her journeys to London and the Lake District. A three-part Christmas special has been ordered. As one of the most experienced execs working in scripted having led the BBC’s drama before launching Bad Wolf, Tranter has made shows such as Doctor Who and Industry . While she acknowledged funding high-end dramas is challenged, she said demand for major series remains strong. “If someone says to you, ‘You can’t make period dramas, no one’s buying them… You can’t make fantasy, no one is buying it.’ You can’t make a drama set in finance. Make it. Just find a way to make it,” she said. As such, Tranter’s Sony-owned Bad Wolf is also known for productions such as Industry , His Dark Materials and Doctor Who , making it one of the UK’s most prolific drama producers across genres of the past decade. James Gandolfini’s influence Earlier in her talk at the Excelsior Westin Hotel in Rome, Tranter played the audience an extended clip of The Night Of , the HBO drama starring Riz Ahmed about a man who is accused of murdering a woman after a one-night stand. Based on a BBC series, Criminal Justice , the series was big hit in 2016 and earned five Emmy wins. She recalled how the HBO production became challenged when James Gandolfini, who had championed the project, unexpectedly passed away while away on holiday in Italy in 2013. He had played Ahmed’s defense lawyer in a pilot and was an exec producer on the show, and his passing left Tranter, then new to the U.S. system having only recently moved from the UK, and series creator Steven Zaillian at a crossroads. “I got really lucky that Steven took on the show, and then I got even luckier that James Gandolfini came in to play the role of John Stone,” she said. “And then James unexpectedly died and the whole project got put on hold for a while. Then, as in life sometimes happens, one door closes and another opens. John Turturro, who is the most brilliant actor and the nicest of men, came in, and so we continued making The Night Of .” Tranter revealed that her experience producing The Night Of also influenced her decision to launch a major production studio in Wales, where the Bad Wolf era of Doctor Who was filmed. “After Jim’s death, I continued to work with a lot of his crew,” she explained. “He was very, very loyal, and his crew were very loyal to him. so a lot of his Sopranos [crew] worked on The Night Of , and I got to know and understand a lot of them from New Jersey. I understood what it was like to work within the community, and I began to think of Wales and the passion of the crews that I had worked with in my time.” Earlier this month, Deadline revealed the production companies vying to become the next producer on Doctor Who when it returns in 2028. Bad Wolf and showrunner Russell T. Davies both dramatically exited in June. Tranter was not quizzed on the current Doctor Who situation on stage. title: Kari Skogland To Direct Vigilante Crime Thriller ‘Vigilant’ From ‘Severance’ Star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Kari Skogland To Direct Vigilante Crime Thriller ‘Vigilant’ From ‘Severance’ Star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson Christie Brinkley Opens Personal Archive With Never-Before-Seen Home Movies For ‘Uptown Girl’ Docuseries Lance Armstrong On Schwinn Bicycles Documentary ‘No Hands’: “It’s An Incredible American Story” View All October 21, 2026 2:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kari Skogland & Ólafur Darri Ólafsson David Leyes, Jonatan Gretarsson EXCLUSIVE: Kari Skogland will direct Vigilant , a vigilante crime thriller based on a Skúli Sigurðsson novel and adapted for TV by Severance star Ólafur Darri Ólafsson . The project is a big-ticket European co-production and has been greenlit by Icelandic production company ACT4 alongside German broadcaster ZDF and its distribution division ZDF Studios . Iceland’s Siminn is also on board. ZDF Studios will sell the English-language show internationally. Zero Gravity is handling U.S. sales. Vigilant follows a female journalist who is approached by a self-styled vigilante who is waging a violent campaign against sexual predators. The reporter initially sees him as a voice for the voiceless, but soon begins to suspect a darker truth. As her reporting fuels a nationwide debate, the series explores whether violence can ever be justified when the justice system fails. Related Stories News Buyers Move For German Crime Drama 'SOKO' As ZDF Studios Brings Classic & YA Series To Cannes News Icelandic Drama 'Elma' Set For Siminn Bow As Glassriver Debuts 'NCU' At MIPCOM Ólafur is a partner in ACT4 and starred in Severance . He has adapted Sigurðsson’s novel ‘Stóri bróðir’ (‘Big Brother’ in English) for TV. Víkingur Kristjánsson, Anita Briem, Teitur Magnússon and Anna Gunndís Guðmundsdóttir are co-writers, meaning a powerhouse Icelandic creative team. Watch on Deadline “Skúli’s novel had a profound impact on me when I first read it,” Ólafur said. “Beneath the thriller, I found a story asking difficult questions about justice, anger and what happens when people lose faith in the systems meant to protect them. “I’m incredibly proud of the scripts we’ve created, and I can’t wait to see Kari bring this world and these characters to life with her extraordinary vision, alongside the incredible cast and creative team we’ve assembled.” Skogland’s many directing credits include The Handmaid’s Tale , The Walking Dead and Vikings . She will also executive produce the six-part series. “ Vigilant captivated me from the first page,” she said. “The characters walk their own lines of morality that continually makes the audience question their own moral position. Everyone’s damage is exposed at some point, their fragility and strength are tested in this fantastic landscape for thought-provoking performance opportunities, all while wrapped in a nail-biting thriller.” “ Vigilant is exactly the kind of premium international drama that resonates across borders: a compelling thriller rooted in a highly relevant societal dilemma,” said Rodrigo Herrera Ibarguengoytia, Director Drama, ZDF Studios. “The series combines Iceland’s distinctive storytelling tradition with universal themes that will connect with audiences worldwide.” Production kicks off on October 29 in Iceland, where the drama is set. ZDF will have the show for Germany and Iceland’s Siminn, which has an IPTV and streaming service, has local rights. full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Watermelon Pictures Acquires North American Distribution Rights To Sara Ishaq’s ‘The Station’ Hiam Abbass To Receive Honorary European Film Academy Award J. Bayona, Javier Bardem & Laurent Bouzereau Partner On Movistar Plus Doc About Life Of Legendary Spanish Cinematographer Néstor Almendros View All October 21, 2026 2:24am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hiam Abbass Deadline Hiam Abbass is set to receive the European Film Academy ’s honorary award for European Achievement in World Cinema. Abbass will be handed the award at the 39th European Film Awards on 16 January 2027 in Athens. She will be the ceremony’s honorary guest. Abbass was born in Nazareth, the child of a Palestinian family that was forced into exile in 1948. She began her acting career at the Palestinian National Theatre El-Hakawati in East Jerusalem, which was often closed by the Israeli authorities. During a theatre tour through Europe, she decided to leave Palestine for London and has been living in Paris since the late 1980s. Related Stories News 'La Bola Negra', 'Woman Unknown', 'NAZA' & 'Fjord' Among 68 Films On Shortlist For 39th European Film Awards Festivals 'Succession' Star Hiam Abbass On How She Had "Real" Connections Working With Kenneth Branagh & Boyd Holbrook On 'Atonement' - TIFF Abbass played her first lead role in 1989 in La nuit miraculeuse directed by Ariane Mnouchkine. She has since acted in over 100 films, including Satin Rouge by Raja Amari, Paradise Now by Hany Abu-Assad, The Visitor by Tom McCarthy, and Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049 . Watch on Deadline Abbass has been nominated twice for European Film Awards, in both cases for her performance in films directed by Eran Riklis: She was nominated for the People’s Choice Award 2005 for Syrian Bride and for European Actress 2008 for Lemon Tree , which won her an Asia Pacific Screen Award. Her daughter Lina Soualem’s documentary Bye Bye Tiberias , which returns to her home village Deir Hanna and explores her bold choices and her bond to her family, was also nominated for the European Film Awards 2024. Alongside her work as an actress, Hiam Abbass also directs. Her film Inheritance was screened at Gijón, São Paulo, and Venice Days (2012). The program of the 50th edition of the festival, which runs through October 29, will include a masterclass with the actor, as well as the presentation of the Leon Cakoff Award, named after the festival founder. On Monday, October 26, the Tony and Emmy winner will take part in a masterclass and receive the Leon Cakoff Award in recognition of his career, presented by Renata de Almeida, director of the festival. Named after the festival’s founder, the award “recognizes distinguished figures in culture and the audiovisual industry.” Screen vet Leguizamo most recently played Eumaeus, Odysseus’ faithful servant and friend, in Christopher Nolan and Universal’s box office juggernaut The Odyssey . title: planned closure of BBC Three
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake BBC Scraps TikTok Generation TV News Bulletin ‘The Catch Up’ Judi Dench Laments “Waste Of Goodwill & Talent” In ‘Cats’: “Oh God, I Can’t Bear It” BBC Three To Be Switched Off For Second Time, As BBC Confirms TV & Radio Network Closures View All October 20, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Fleabag' launched on BBC Three Bye bye BBC Three — again. The BBC will pull the plug on BBC Three for the second time in a decade in spring 2027, as the UK broadcaster confirmed network closures under plans to save £500 million ($666M). Deadline first revealed last month that BBC Three , the youth network that has given rise to beloved British series including Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey , was in serious jeopardy. The BBC originally planned to reveal the closures in late September, but the corporation delayed confirmation as it managed the timing of various cuts announcements across the organization. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Acquisitions The BBC & MHz Choice Board Sweden's Latest 'Wallander' Series News BBC News Slashing 100 Jobs: "This Will Be Very Difficult For Those Affected" The BBC has confirmed that BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra will also close as linear networks in spring next year. Deadline first reported that Radio 4 Extra was at risk earlier this month. It marks another brutal day for the British broadcaster, which also announced 100 layoffs in its news division over the coming months, saving £5.5M. BBC Three will remain a brand on iPlayer, and the BBC has committed to increasing investment for younger audiences. BBC Scotland will also be retained on iPlayer. In a memo to staff setting out the changes, BBC director-general Matt Brittin said: “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices.” He added: “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues.” The BBC’s decision marks the second time BBC Three has been taken off air in the past 10 years. It was originally moved online in 2016 before former director general Tim Davie reversed the decision and the channel was restored to television in 2022. Although BBC Three’s move to iPlayer was ahead of its time (a fact that was acknowledged by the BBC at the time), Davie’s U-turn bemused many — particularly as the network enjoyed a purple patch creatively online, launching series including beloved comedies Fleabag and This Country . BBC Three is now home to shows like RuPaul’s Drag Race UK , which was recently canceled by the BBC , and comedies including Things You Should Have Done and Smoggie Queens . BBC Three falls under the remit of Kate Phillips, the corporation’s chief content officer. Fiona Campbell was the controller of the network until earlier this year, when she was promoted to director of factual content. The BBC’s £500M target expands on a previous savings goal worth £1.5 billion. The bigger picture behind the cuts is that 94% of the UK population use the BBC every month, but fewer than 80% pay the £180 annual licence fee. The BBC is attempting to bridge this gap. Up to 2,000 jobs are at risk under the savings strategy, while the BBC is also involved in tense negotiations with unions over employee pay rises . Unions have rejected two BBC offers, increasing the threat of industrial action. The drumbeat of BBC cuts has been playing for weeks, with the broadcaster canceling shows including Radio 4’s You and Yours ; axing sports bulletins; and making 110 layoffs in BBC Media Tech , the division that powers online services like iPlayer. BBC commissioners have also been asked to consider applying for voluntary redundancy, per an email seen by Deadline. The BBC is slashing costs at the same time as executives are locked in talks with the government over renewing the corporation’s charter. Weekly meetings are taking place between government officials and BBC policy staff as they thrash out the broadcaster’s future funding arrangements.
